It's working in development server but for some reason I still get logged out in casper tests.

I think the race condition is between `/json/events` and `/json/settings/change` calls.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-02-21 11:01 UTC

So I was able to use the Django's DB backend API for both PostgreSQL and SQLAlchemy. This removes a lot of code related to time tracking and query logging from our codebase which is now handled by Django. It also gives us the advantage of using Django's `CaptureQueriesContext` to capture queries for both SQLAlchemy and Postgres. Both SQLAlchemy and Postgres can now be accessed using the same Django API like this:
```Python
from django.db import connections
connections['default']  # Postgres connection
connections['sqlalchemy']   # SQLAlchemy connection
```
(I still need to clean some code)
Code for this is at #3367.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-02-23 04:08 UTC

@Tim Abbott, Django doesn't have a SQLAlchemy backend. Django provides base classes ([PostgreSQL DatabaseWrapper](https://github.com/django/django/blob/master/django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py#L61), [BaseDatabaseWrapper](https://github.com/django/django/blob/master/django/db/backends/base/base.py#L24), [CursorDebugWrapper](https://github.com/django/django/blob/master/django/db/backends/utils.py#L71)) which can be used to create a custom backend. I used the PostgreSQL backend as the base class to wrap the code we had in `zerver/lib/sqlalchemy_utils.py` with it. So essentially we will still be using our old old but through Django's backend API.
I can create detailed documentation for this.

We have moved to a new design in #5880. Basically now we will pass a wrapper object to the functions. So now while calling the rate limiter API we will pass `WrapperObject(user)` instead of `User`. * There should not be a lot of changes in the already written API.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-15 08:06 UTC

Some comments on `AutoField` to `BigAutoField` migration (PR #6105):

On a large dataset this migration will be slow. Mainly because Postgresql alters column by first creating a new row and then deleting the old row and with constraints this becomes a slow operation for large tables. It seems that the fastest method is to create a new table, move data to the new table, drop the old table, rename the new table and then add the constraints.

The drop column operation is fast because it just makes the column invisible. To free the actual disk space you need to do a one time slow operation using VACUUM FULL or let the space be reclaimed over time as the rows are updated.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-15 08:13 UTC

>it seems that the fastest method is to create a new table, move data to the new table, drop the old table, rename the new table and then add the constraints.

I think we can also change the sequence to this:
1. Create a new table.
2. Move data to the new table.
3. Apply all the constraints.
4. Make Django use the new table using `Model.Meta.db_table`.
5. Delete the old table.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-15 08:24 UTC

Nicely summarizes: https://www.braintreepayments.com/blog/safe-operations-for-high-volume-postgresql/

So I spent some time investigating the issue of running backend tests with Python3.5 in Travis. It seems that virtualenv is created with Python3.4 even though `python3` points to Python3.5 in Travis. When we activate the venv the path is set for Python3.5 but that doesn't exist. This build has the debugging info to highlight the issue: https://travis-ci.org/zulip/zulip/builds/270319897?utm_source=github_status&utm_medium=notification

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-31 20:06 UTC

This looks like a cause of the issue:

> Aug 31 08:19:07 + sudo virtualenv -p python3 /home/travis/zulip-venv-cache/85e8341de67de621813f24f210052898216b80f3/zulip-py3-venv
> Aug 31 08:19:08 Running virtualenv with interpreter /usr/bin/python3

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-31 20:07 UTC

The interpreter at `/usr/bin/python3` is the one from the system, which is going to be Python 3.4 because this is a `trusty` system. What we want is for that `virtualenv` command to use the `python3` from the 3.5 virtualenv that Travis has set up for us.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-01 04:22 UTC

Yeah. It seems that virtualenv doesn't pick the interpreter from another virtualenv. Travis enables Python 3.5 through a virtualenv and `python3` does point to that virtualenv if you do `which python3` but when you create the virtualenv with `-p python3`, it refers the system Python.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-01 04:23 UTC

This clears the situation:
```
Sep 01 04:11:00 + which python3
Sep 01 04:11:00 /home/travis/virtualenv/python3.5.3/bin/python3
Sep 01 04:11:00 + python3 --version
Sep 01 04:11:00 Python 3.5.3
Sep 01 04:11:00 + python --version
Sep 01 04:11:00 Python 3.5.3
Sep 01 04:11:00 ****************************************************************************************************
Sep 01 04:11:00 ['-p', 'python3']


# We activate the virtualenv here.
Sep 01 04:11:00 + python3 --version
Sep 01 04:11:00 Python 3.4.3
Sep 01 04:11:00 + python --version
Sep 01 04:11:00 Python 3.4.3
Sep 01 04:11:00 ['python3.4']
```

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-05 08:12 UTC

I have submitted a PR #6401 for fixing our multiline i18n strings. It mainly tries to make sure that the string argument in the `i18n.t` function is on a single line. The problem with using string concatenation is that '+' is also captured. So if the string is:

```
i18n.t('one ' + two + ' three');
```
we will send 
```
'one' + two  + ' three'
```
 for translation.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-14 08:13 UTC

File based mutex is ready. PR #6338. Would like to add some tests for this.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-14 08:17 UTC

The reason for this mutex:

    We need to protect password updates for two reasons:

    - Development server runs under a multi-threaded environment.
    - Tornado event system accesses user session from a separate process.
    
    The problem occurs when a password change is in process and session is
    accessed before user session hash is written to DB. This commit
    implements a file based mutex which serializes session access when
    password change is in progress. If the access is in another thread of
    Zulip web application we block for a small amount of time. If the access
    is in Tornado event system we return without blocking and restart the
    request at a later time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-14 11:09 UTC

@Umair Khan hmm, I'm not sure about this file-based mutex concept.  We certainly can't use it in production, since Tornado and Django should be able to be run on different servers from each other.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-14 11:09 UTC

But if this fixes the casper problem, I could imagine having this mutex that exists only in development for making the Casper testing work well with password changes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-14 11:10 UTC

The other thing that we could do, that might be cleaner, is to refresh the user's session inside the `change_password` in-browser route, so that the user doesn't get the current session logged out when they change their password, which is probably what we want.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 03:59 UTC

I see. Makes sense. How about we use a memcached based lock? Even if the lock is flushed out the worst case scenario is just the user getting logged out.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 08:13 UTC

Well, I'm a bit worried about adding locking here, because the Tornado process is very performance-sensitive.  Like, right now, I believe it does exactly 1 memcached query to authorize a user request in the general case.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 08:15 UTC

OK. Perhaps then we should only add this lock in dev and Travis?

Yeah, I think we should try just doing a file lock only for testing, assuming it actually fixes the Casper issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-06 23:37 UTC

Root cause is that we were for some reason using a memcached cache to manage which static files the current version should be using, rather than a fixed manifest

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-07 00:21 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-07 00:22 UTC

so it could be that usually the old values were being flushed

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-07 00:22 UTC

But I think the main thing is that for our deployments on e.g. chat.zulip.org, we're using `upgrade-zulip-from-git`, which builds the static assets on the server and thus was probably replacing the value in memcached as part of that build process

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-07 00:23 UTC

I think this explains a weird failure mode I saw once where just running `update-prod-static` on chat.zulip.org with an experimental new version brought the server down unexpectedly

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-11 05:19 UTC

Some of my takeaways from the event:
* We should probably adjust our policy towards handling of old+inactive PRs (even if they're useful) to close more of them to reduce clutter.  One can always pull them out of the history, and it's very rare for folks to come back to a PR they abandoned 6 months ago.
* We're doing really well compared to a lot of large projects in terms of keeping our issue tracker manageable and responding quickly to contributions.  Something to keep up, since a lot of other important projects also complain they have a hard time onboarding new contributors :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-11 05:20 UTC

* I learned about a few events that we might want to have a presence at, such as Write / Speak / Code.

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-10-11 05:24 UTC

**Trent Lapinski** · 2020-12-02 02:07 UTC

2-4 weeks is average quarantine depending on how sick people get and how many people are involved. Most of the people I know who have had it required 3-6 weeks to get better. However, you're only really contagious in the first 14 days or so or when you have a fever. Where things get complicated is when there's multiple people involved like in Tim's situation. His daughter seems to have gotten it first, then Tim got it about a week later. So the quarantine date starts over now that Tim has symptoms. So he's looking at 3 weeks as of right now (the week that's already passed, and the new 2 week period starting as of yesterday when he first got symptoms). If his wife or other baby present with symptoms at all in the next 2 weeks then their total quarantine period could get pushed out further. Plus the virus lives on surfaces for several days. So realistically, they're looking at about 3-4 weeks currently, but that could change.

**Alicja Raszkowska** · 2016-10-28 06:36 UTC

I didn't mean changing the same components, rather introducing a feature that changes different files intercontextually

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-28 06:41 UTC

I didn't mean changing the same components either (the `components.css` filename is probably a bit misleading).  I was also talking about intercontextual changes.  If that situation arises where we have styling coupled between five different components in some way, and we can't do it in separate atomic commits, then I think we're going to have some kind of design problem that transcends file organization.  But, long story short, I like having separate small files for lots of reasons, so I think the current changes are great, and I'd be cautious about moving back to one big file with "sections."

**Alicja Raszkowska** · 2016-10-28 06:42 UTC

I think we'll find a good balance at some point :)

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-28 06:42 UTC

agreed :)

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-28 06:47 UTC

In my experience 150 lines of code is a good dividing line.  By the time a component has 150 lines of code it's very hard to accuse it of being overly atomic.  You don't necessarily need to split it up immediately, but after about 150 lines of code it's "carrying it's weight" and you can stop feeling guilty about it being too granular.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-28 06:50 UTC

And `compose.css` is 471 lines of code, to give an example of something that I think meets the balance.  That feels self-contained enough to me to be split out, and I definitely would not feel any urge to merge it back with other stuff.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-21 16:19 UTC

One thing that you can do when setting up a ssh key is to attach a passcode to it.  If you use a passcode, in some ways you lose the convenience of not having to type a password, but the OS can usually remember it for you.  The combo of passcode-plus-private-key is more secure than having a password, because even if somebody guess your passcode, they still need your private key, and vice versa.

All of the tests need to set the name of the stream in basically two places, it's just kind of hidden in some places.  An example here would be StashHookTests. something like this:

```
git rm <oops-file>
git commit -am "removed"
git rebase -i HEAD~2

```

**Vishnu KS** · 2019-12-27 17:43 UTC

I have been working this week mostly on making Zulip archive run on GitHub actions. With archive running on GitHub actions, users no longer need a server for running the archive script. The action can be deployed in any GitHub repo in a few click. It would update the repo periodically to be in sync with the choosen Zulip server and trigger GitHub page builds. See https://github.com/hackerkid/zulip-archive-action-test-2 for a demo. The code for the action can be found at https://github.com/hackerkid/zulip-archive-action. The work remaining is getting the code for action merged into zulip-archive repositary, documentation, publishing the action in GitHub app store and cleaning up some code + fixing some  minor bugs.

Yup. Actions do support scheduling and you can use the cron syntax for configuring it. The zulip archive repo above is running at 20 miniutes. More details here

**Umair Khan** · 2017-02-24 03:51 UTC

>We should probably discuss #1760 a bit on #backend. I'm thinking that for fields that are part of the "core" user profile, they should just be first-class columns in UserProfile, rather than a JSONField.

I think creating a separate model to handle profile fields also works. I am not super excited about maintaining these fields solely through a JSONField because then we let go of all the DB safeguards like uniqueness etc. JSONField for me will be a performance feature for reducing read latency. 

Adding profile fields directly on UserProfile won't be flexible enough.

I was actually thinking of the following architecture:
```Python
class ProfileField(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)  # type: Text
    field_type = models.CharField(max_length=100, unique=True)  # type: Text
    realm = models.ForeignKey(Realm)

    def as_dict(self):
        # type: () -> Dict[Text, Text]
        return {
            'id': self.id,
            'name': self.name,
            'type': self.field_type,
        }
class UserProfile(models.Model):
# other fields
profile_fields = JSONField(default=list)
```
The realm administrator will make changes to `ProfileField` table and `UserProfile.profile_fields` will be equal to `[field.as_dict() for field in Realm.profilefield_set.all()]`.

@Puneeth Chaganti answered pretty much all your questions. I kind of typed this so posting anyway. Netlify and Surge is not comparable to Heroku as they serve only static files. **Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-20 03:32 UTC

do you have a sense for how far we are from being done with circular dependency work?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-20 03:48 UTC

definitely weeks...I think the plan is basically this:
* spend some time cleaning up stuff that just needs to be better organized, using circular dependencies as a red flag
* find some clean way to fix circular dependencies that aren't really structurally flawed, but just not easy to load in order (think popovers and modals)
* do really dirty back-door stuff for things that are just hard to fix right away, so that we can proceed with webpack or other similar things

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-20 03:51 UTC

I think we'll eventually want some kind of service-registration system that is not quite as dirty/global as triggers, but which allows us to work around some modules being both sources and sinks.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-20 03:54 UTC

To use popovers as an example, popovers would load after all the modules it dispatches to, but then it would register it's show/hide methods in some kind of global singleton service object that other modules can use.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-20 04:04 UTC

Cool, good to know.  The graph doesn't look too thorny now, but I guess that gives us credit for a ton of future work?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-20 04:08 UTC

yep, it definitely gives us credit for future work...it's kinda hard to predict at this point...adding in one module can make the graph explode, which can be glass half empty (dependencies compound) or glass half full (fixing one module can make a huge difference)

I have a question. When someone is offline and is mentioned, is the email sent immediately?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-03 20:14 UTC

No, there's up to a two-minute delay, and during that window, things can happen like the message gets deleted (in which case we ignore the message) or multiple messages can arrive for a user (in which case we aggregate).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-03 20:16 UTC

The two-minute delay, however, is a little bit non-deterministic relative to when an original message gets sent, so long term we want to make the timing a bit more rigorous.  (The two-minute interval happens at the queue processing level, and it's not really on a per-message basis.)

**Shayan Toqraee** · 2017-10-03 21:37 UTC

I asked this because I had a bad experience a few times. I sent a message that included a mention, and then I found out that there is a typo, or something wrong with the message. And before I could edit it, the email was sent.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-03 21:40 UTC

Yeah, it's tricky.  Part of the motivation for sending missed-message emails is that we want people to be able to know that they didn't miss out in a timely fashion, so, for example, they don't hop on the train right before they find they need to go back into the office.  But it's also annoying when they go out too fast.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-03 21:41 UTC

I think it's probably worth opening an issue for making the email delay more deterministic.  I think we could without too much trouble make it "nearly exactly 2 minutes".

**Greg Price** · 2021-10-12 19:29 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell (showell))
> Tim told me a somewhat funny story about this. Apparently the mobile app has long I had this feature working in development mode. The idea was that developers wanted to test stuff without messing with the unread counts.
> But the feature was never turned on for the rest of the world.
> It turns out to be a useful feature in general. :-)

Yeah. The feature was actually in release builds, so available for anyone in principle… but because it was intended as a debug feature:
* the switch for it was tucked into a "debug" section of settings;
* it would reset when you restarted the app;
* in the message list, the unread indicators at the left side would still disappear just as if we were marking the messages as read -- which would have been awfully disconcerting if you were trying to use this as a real feature :smile: 

(The last bit was actually not so much a matter of not having polished the feature, as it was part of its intended debugging purpose: IIRC the last time we really used this debugging feature was for bugs in the algorithm for deciding what to mark as read, before we overhauled that algorithm in #M3040. For that use case, you want the animation telling you what would be marked as read, but want them not *actually* marked as read so you can immediately repro the same situation by navigating out and back in.)

**Greg Price** · 2021-10-12 19:30 UTC

The spiffy new actually-a-feature version of this feature was added by @Akash Dhiman in #M4880.

When I touch type, I use the ring finger to hit the l key, and I feel something, which is good, but it's not the best feeling either, since there's a tiny twinge.

I am confident enough that things are improving that I'm not gonna go the route of voice recognition or one-handed keyboards, but I will instead focus on normal ergonomic improvements like buying a better two handed keyboard.  My sister actually had a very similar issue a couple years ago, and she said simple things like better keyboards helped.  She actually had it more severe than me, and hers lasted several months.

**Robert Hönig** · 2018-05-31 06:47 UTC

Also, I got a response:

 > You're absolutely right, the explicitly written out 2019 triggered a translation check (as if 2019 was a real number, not part of the unicode). Translation checks can be of different severity level: either just a warning, when you can still save translations with no problem, or an error message: https://docs.transifex.com/setup/setting-translation-checks
When it's set as a warning, you should still be able to save your translations. I would recommend contacting your Transifex project maintainer/administrator to change the severity of translation checks, if it doesn't allow you to save the translations due to this issue.

* For existing priorities, I think any of those should be covered under the "generic issues.md" task type.  For larger things like the "User groups UI", we might want to split it into a few tasks, since it's a larger project.  I think there's unlikely to be a fairness risk there, because these larger projects are generally all too big to be a GCI task.
* Since task count is mostly used for who is in the top 10 (whereas the winners are chosen based on overall contributions), I would encourage doing what you might naturally do (helping other students, working on more complex tasks, etc.).  
* Since you're going to be mostly away the first week, I think the things I'd be most worried about (clearing out everything in a task category that was good for beginners early on) are unlikely to come up, but I guess that'd what I'd appreciate your avoiding :).  But halfway through the competition, we're unlikely to get many more beginners, so at that point you could certainly try to finish areas (it's nice for us when that happens, since we don't need to keep track of that area for post-GCI work).

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-27 18:00 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> It didn’t capture the data in advance. It’s proxying requests to the actual server in real time.

From the screenshot Aman posted in the next message, it looks like the register request went to https://web.archive.org/web/20220602093559/https://chat.zulip.org/json/register .

That's an archived URL that has a timestamp from 2022-06-02 in it, the same timestamp that's on the overall page capture. The semantics of that URL should be that it's always data from the time of that capture, not from some later request to the actual server.

So that seems to me like something that's accurately described as having captured the data in advance, rather than as proxying anything in real time.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-27 18:26 UTC

https://web.archive.org/web/20220602093559/https://chat.zulip.org/json/register redirects to
https://web.archive.org/web/20220602093504/https://chat.zulip.org/json/register.

If I cause it to fetch new messages by scrolling, narrowing, or typing a unique query into the Zulip search bar, I get a JSON request to
https://web.archive.org/web/20220602093559/https://chat.zulip.org/json/messages?…foo… redirecting to
https://web.archive.org/save/_embed/https://chat.zulip.org/json/messages?…foo… redirecting to
https://web.archive.org/web/20220627181646/https://chat.zulip.org/json/messages?…foo… with today’s date.

It didn’t anticipate my actions in advance. If we turned off the real chat.zulip.org tomorrow (or changed the API), the only actions that would appear to be functional on the archived page are the ones exactly matching actions previous visitors took on the archived page.

It’s up to you whether you want to call that “archiving” or “proxying”, but for the purpose of this conversation, the relevant thing is that search engines don’t work that way.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-27 18:33 UTC

(But I dunno, maybe they will in five years when Google is allowed to achieve its browser monopoly and there will be nobody left to fight when they start proxying all your clicks through the Google crawlers.)

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-02 19:37 UTC

Both Flow and TypeScript offer similar benefits, and it is quite clear that one of them should be used for the web app. 
Flow is easier to introduce gradually, while TypeScript has better tooling and type definitions for 3rd party libraries.
While I am quite happy with TypeScript being chosen for the web app, there is a benefit to both web app and mobile app using the same type infrastructure. Not sure how viable it is to switch to TypeScript for a React Native project.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-12 14:15 UTC

@Joshua Pan One sort of general comment about testing is that we want to avoid things like this, when possible, for setting up data:

~~~
view._rows[id] = '#row_' + id;
~~~

It's generally better if you can use the API to set up data, and verify "round trip" behavior.  I've violated this rule myself, sometimes for expediency but sometimes for more subtle reasons.  Like if the API to insert data is complicated, it can make sense to just use the internal method.  Or sometimes you're trying to get test coverage on error handlinig from theoretical states that violate our invariants.  But I'm not sure  that's going on here.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-12 14:20 UTC

Another factor to consider here is that lots of the existing MLV node tests were written before we split out MessageListData, so there might be some kind of janky helpers that could possibly be a bit more clean now.  I haven't looked in depth.  Your first commit to move them to the top of the file definitely makes sense.  But be aware as you get deeper into this that you may be able to come back and simplify a few things.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-12 14:24 UTC

One other sort of "meta" thing is that you write tests for MLV, you'll notice certain aspects of the module are hard to test, while others are easy.  There's not a 100% correlation between good design and testability, but they often go hand in hand, and tests should make you think about the code's structure.  (The one place where there's a tradeoff is that private messages are good design, but occasionally make it harder to test, but even then, it's more of a thought question, as a good public API in a small cohesive module should be enough for most tests, or perhaps having to make private methods more public suggests there's an "interior" component that actually deserves to be its own class.)

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2018-05-23 16:49 UTC

I couldn't understand what "resolving JSON references in YAML files" meant. Can somebody explain or point me to an example, to help me understand?

**Yago González** · 2018-05-23 16:50 UTC

Sure, @Puneeth Chaganti! Say you have the following YAML file:

~~~yaml
        default:
          description: unexpected error
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Error"
components:
  schemas:
    Error:
      required:
        - code
        - message
      properties:
        code:
          type: integer
          format: int32
        message:
          type: string
~~~

The JSON reference is the `$ref` tag, and by "resolving" it I mean replacing that tag with whatever it's pointing at.

**Yago González** · 2018-05-23 16:51 UTC

In this case, you'd be left with something like:

~~~yaml
default:
          description: unexpected error
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                required:
                  - code
                  - message
                properties:
                  code:
                    type: integer
                    format: int32
                  message:
                    type: string
~~~

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2018-05-23 16:52 UTC

Thanks for the example, @Yago González !

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-09-21 02:22 UTC

Updated #P124 with some major changes. Here's what things look like, if you run:
```
./tools/release_packages.py 0.3.5 --build --release --push origin --cleanup
```
the following things would happen:

1. The versions will be automatically incremented to 0.3.5 in all `__init__.py` files.
2. `--build`: Source distributions and universal wheels would be generated under `<package_dir>/dist/`.
3. `--release`: Everything under the `dist/` directories previously mentioned would be uploaded to PyPA using `twine`.
4. `--push origin`: A new branch will be checked out, changes made in Step 1 will be committed and pushed to your local fork (origin). Can also be `--push upstream`, in which case, `master` will be checked out and changes made in Step 1 will be committed and pushed upstream.
5. `--cleanup`: Once all is said and done, this cleans up all directories created by the build commands, making sure you don't accidentally release older and outdated dists the next time you make a release.

Next thing I'd like to add is to update `requirements` in the main repo, commit the change, and push automatically without any intervention on my part. This would lead to a one-command solution to making a release. And a release would not take more than 2-3 minutes!

@Tim Abbott: I'd really appreciate some initial feedback before I work on this further! Thanks! :blush:

**Greg Price** · 2018-01-31 02:26 UTC

I definitely think that in the medium to long term, we should offer an option to install Zulip with docker-compose. If it makes things better for a common situation, we should offer the same for the dev environment.

The tricky thing in both of those will be to keep the docker-compose-based setup and the more traditional-Unix-server setup as closely aligned as possible -- everything that the two of them do separately, we'll have double the opportunities for stuff to break and double the maintenance to do to keep them both working.

**Greg Price** · 2018-01-31 18:25 UTC

Vagrant doesn't actually manage VMs itself -- it just spits out some config files for the things that actually do. On Linux, we have the magic of containers, and LXC is definitely the recommended way to run the dev environment today. If you're using LXC, you're getting the exact same technology from the kernel that Docker uses, and you should see similar benefits in CPU and memory use.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-03-25 07:30 UTC

If you do need to start compiling kernels, it helps to generate a minimal kernel config using `make localmodconfig`.

Here’s the config snippet I used for a recent kernel bisection:

```nix
boot.kernelPackages = pkgs.recurseIntoAttrs (pkgs.linuxPackagesFor
  (pkgs.linux_5_11.override {
    argsOverride = {
      modDirVersion = "5.9.0-rc4";
      src = /home/anders/linux;
    };
    structuredExtraConfig =
      import ./kernel-config.nix { inherit (pkgs.lib.kernel) no; };
    ignoreConfigErrors = true;
  }));
```

where `kernel-config.nix` is

```nix
{ no }:

{
  "60XX_WDT" = no;
  "6LOWPAN" = no;
  "8139CP" = no;
  "8139TOO" = no;
  ABP060MG = no;
  ACENIC = no;
  ACERHDF = no;
  ACER_WIRELESS = no;
  …
  ZOPT2201 = no;
  ZPA2326 = no;
  ZSMALLOC = no;
  ZX_TDM = no;
}
```

However, I'd appreciate feedback on two other issues:
* get_queue_client() (line 83) is essentially a singleton constructor? It is specified to return not-None, but the function does not ensure this (at least explicitly) but presumably depends upon settings.USINGRABBITMQ always being set. Does this warrant a mypy ignore? Is this related to testing?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-08 17:34 UTC

I think the queue stuff is going to be really hard to make mypy happy with without significant refactoring.  At least for the channel, we can only assume that the client isn't None after `ensure_queue` has been called.  Probably a good test case for the mypy developers CC @Greg Price .

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-10 21:09 UTC

@Neil Pilgrim Yeah, I'll be interested to dig into that one!

Without yet looking at the code, in general one good way to handle a case where something is non-None but for subtle reasons (too subtle for the type-checker to see) is to add an `assert`. Where applicable, that tends to be a pretty great solution -- even apart from the type-checker, it makes what's really going on clearer to a human reader. The main way that solution can break down is where there isn't a good one or two places for the assert, and you'd have to add lots of asserts in a bunch of places, which isn't so helpful for readability.

**Greg Price** · 2019-03-19 23:57 UTC

In particular, I had a talk to give midday Sunday (the last of 3 conference days at PyCon), and I decided... I think it was actually Saturday afternoon, i.e. less than 24hr in advance, that I wanted to make major changes to its organization and content. (From talking to random people at the conference, I'd significantly updated my model of what the audience currently knew and thought.)

I'd also heard reveal.js mentioned the previous day by a friend I know gives good talks, as what they use. That was the first I'd heard of it. The slides I had were in Dropbox Paper, which has a low ceiling on how polished or finely-tuned your slides can get.

So I converted my slides from Dropbox Paper to reveal.js, and also made all the substantive changes I wanted to make. And it worked out well!

**Greg Price** · 2019-03-19 23:58 UTC

As part of that release, I've been exploring using the 'milestone' feature in github for releases - it's helped a little so far, both in terms of preliminary prioritizing of issues for next release, but also tracking which issues/PRs go into a release. The minor nuances are that
* occasionally things don't go through a PR
* some issues are fixed by a PR, so there's duplication

Have other people tried GH milestones?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-23 17:43 UTC

We used GitHub milestones for tracking release work for a release or two around Zulip Server 1.8; we found it to be a lot of overhead and moved to the `priority` labels system instead.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-23 17:44 UTC

Basically because deciding what release to put something in is a decision that is coupled to complex questions around what the release schedule is, who's likely to be able to work on this, etc.; whereas marking something as important doesn't require answering those questions.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-07-23 18:00 UTC

I agree it's duplication - the commits being present in a branch typically define a release, and having commit->PR/issue connections would be simpler. Also each issue/PR can only be in one milestone, so it doesn't work if something went into eg. a stable *and* backport release. The same could be achieved with release labels (and with more flexibility?), it's just that you'd need to dig through the labels rather than having the 'milestone' namespace.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2023-03-10 00:09 UTC

My recent merged work on zulip-terminal has been focused on documentation, infrastructure & maintenance:
- Clarifying, rewording and expanding the README and FAQs
- Migrating from `flake8` to `ruff`, and enabling sets of rules incrementally
- Adding `codespell` to linting, and investigating `typos`
- Migrating tooling to use a centralized `pyproject.toml`
- Introducing job dependency and commit isolation into CI
- Migrating from 3.6-3.10 to 3.7-3.11 range of Python, then upgrading many dependencies
- Refactoring older code, including the historically-complex ZT entry-point

Other than a fix for a bug reported today, recently I have a large branch which is an extension of the last point which will involve extracting our `zuliprc`-handling code and significantly improving its testing and readability, which may have some utility in python-zulip-api or perhaps as an additional package.

I also have various branches underway that aren't up to date, which I'd like to return to, but were interrupted when working on GSoC or other more important tasks.

Ah, true, I should really have said 'has slot(s)'; I was mainly trying to distinguish from so many computers these days that have only soldered-in RAM. Both my current laptop (1 slot, was 8G) and the mini-desktop (2 slots, was 1x8G) use DDR4 SODIMMs, so a split-up "paired 2x32G" replaced the 8G in my laptop and filled a slot in the mini-desktop, yet could later be used together in another machine together (in case memory decides it 'needs' to be paired, which I doubt).

These computers are both second-hand, for a fraction of the original price, and now have more RAM than either manufacturer manual claims they support! - #T1376 Use server_timestamp for presences :hammer_and_wrench: Data ordering affects existing design
- #T1345 Latest combined rebase of various solarized dark work :git-pull-request-draft: Pulling latest work together, so someone else may take forward
- #T1334 Highlight current narrow; rebase/rework of #T1244 (originally by @Progyan) :hammer_and_wrench: Needs refactor/tests
- #T1324 Migrate fully to pyproject.toml :hammer_and_wrench: Needs update, but has consequences for eg. CI to resolve

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-06 19:14 UTC

In the right situation that can be much more readable than either a single giant regex, or plain JS (or Python or whatever) code with no regexes.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-06 19:19 UTC

One example of this is in the zulipVersion.js file that @Chris Bobbe recently added in the mobile codebase, where it parses Zulip server version strings. First there's a regex for the part that's like 2.1.2; then for the optional -dev or -rcN; then for the optional -42-gabcd01234. Each of those is pretty readable, and a lot more so than if you tried to write the same thing where `(\d+)` and so on were expanded out into loops.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-06 19:19 UTC

(deleted)

**Chris Bobbe** · 2020-03-06 20:03 UTC

Thanks for mentioning that, Greg! :slight_smile: That's #M3839.

I think an important fact that helped convinced me to break it up in that case was that we didn't have to make an all-or-nothing decision on the shape of the entire string.

Because of the nature of the version string, where it increases in granularity from left to right, it was OK to start at the beginning and accumulate useful bits of information, and if something didn't match, we could stop looking and return what we'd gathered so far — with the consequence that we had *some* knowledge about the version, just perhaps not very precise knowledge. This fits nicely with the strategy of checking for one pattern, then another, and another, etc., and returning early when one doesn't match.

In a different project, unrelated to Zulip, I've had to match some (happily!) very well-specified strings encoded in barcodes (one was [GS1-128](https://www.barcode.graphics/education-gs1-128-barcode/)). But in such a case, even if 99% of the data was well-formed, we were required to reject *entirely* when the slightest bit of garbage appeared anywhere in the string. When that's necessary, it can be really reassuring to use a single pattern beginning with `^` and ending with `$`, and match on the entire string in one go — otherwise, if you're handling it with multiple patterns and custom code, it's up to you to handle the control flow correctly to make sure no garbage gets missed, and it may not be as obvious when you've accomplished that. For one of those barcode formats, I think we took advantage of the fact that a pattern itself can be constructed with a string, and we split up that string into chunks, which we concatenated and passed to `new RegExp`, or something like that.

Obviously, Zulip messages are much more flexible than international standards for encoding data, so I don't see any obvious impediments to breaking up a giant regex into multiple regexes.

There are two things that I can recommend that may help a wee bit.
One: make sure that the lighting of your workspace is proper - you don't want glare off of your screen nor do you want too much or too little light in your room - if I get the lighting wrong or look at my screen from the wrong angle for too long, I end up getting some pretty bad headaches sometimes, mainly originating from the back of my eye and the temples. In fact sometimes the headache can get so bad that I'd feel nauseous.
Two: try the 20-20-20 rule: Every 20 minutes look at something 20 meters away for 20 seconds.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-15 23:07 UTC

As a cautionary tale on that front: a close friend ignored wrist pain for a week playing computer games with a friend over the holidays one year, and in that week up injuring his wrists badly enough he had to use voice software to type for the next year.

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-15 23:12 UTC

In addition to lighting, one variable I'd recommend paying attention to is posture -- how your head and neck sit when you're at the computer.

It's very common when sitting at a computer to end up in a posture with your head and shoulders both pushed forward and down from their most natural position. There's a complex system of a lot of different muscles holding everything in place, and in that position some muscles get tense and tight. In particular the trapezius, which wraps around the neck, down to the front and back of the shoulders, and up to the back of the head.

Then there are lots of different problems that can cause. One that's not so common but can happen is... migraine headaches.

**Trent Lapinski** · 2020-06-16 02:33 UTC

It's been giving me headaches, and making it hard to play games, etc. I started missing my shots in Fortnite, and realized if I aimed with my left eye I would make my shots, but if aimed with both or my right I was missing. Anyhow, its something to look into. Didn't even consider astigmatism in just one of my eyes. Kind of sucks I need glasses for 1 eye, they don't make contacts for astigmatism for my prescription. I have mostly been having issues with contrasts with the bad eye.

Try covering one eye, and looking at your screen, then switch and cover the other eye. If there's a significant difference or one is blurry or doubled it puts strain on both eyes and your brain trying to correct the image in your head which can lead to headaches. You probably need to see an eye doctor and get it diagnosed and see what's up. You might need glasses or if you have them currently a change in prescription.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-05-04 15:57 UTC

I am hoping to find something in the blog posts by dropbox otherwise most likely we will have to allow inline styles without nonce approach (because nonce disables inline styles which don't have a nonce and using js to insert styles exactly does that)

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-05-06 13:42 UTC

so at the end I ended up dropping the nonce approach for styles which would have meant no inline styles (which is very hard to not have). I added a few other directives to the commit in PR #9065 and did a test deploy on nightly. Of course its still in report only mode and we probably need to do more testing in this mode and see what kinda of errors we see in reports from clients.
Next on the CSP front is investigate more into `'unsafe-eval'` in the `script-src`. From what I have seen we won't actually won't be able to completely drop unsafe-eval from our csp policy due to its use in 3rd party libs. 
Even dropbox ended up retaining the unsafe-evals (due to some of the legacy templates plus 3rd party libs) but they did patch Jquery to make stuff bit more safe and shared the patch [here](https://gist.github.com/devd/e23de63265f00c0550c4). So next thing is most likely see what we can do about that patch (dropbox did all this stuff around 2015 so definitely stuff has changed since then) and investigate the unsafe-evals more.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-05-06 20:29 UTC

So after pursuing the csp in main app without unsafe-eval a bit more, it turns out most of the violation reports I was seeing in development (in bootstap.js?) go away when we try the same policy in prod.
Turns out webpack has some hand in that mainly the devtool option being set to (`cheap-module-eval-source-map` or `eval` for that matter. Also see [this](https://medium.com/@indolent.dev/webpack-unsafe-eval-nightmare-3813d8e5beca))

Now the reports after removing unsafe eval which are left over in prod are relating to some `addScript.js` which indeed is again a part of webpack system. To be exact part of a loader called `script-loader` which is run by webpack. Purpose of this loader is to run every script once in the global scope. I am not really sure now if this one can be dealt with because to execute all the scripts the loader uses the eval function.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-05-06 20:46 UTC

Good thing here is it seems like Jquery indeed has become csp compatible as far as unsafe-evals go. Basically evals seem to have been removed, or it maybe I haven't triggered any yet! Looking at this issues [page](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/issues?utf8=%E2%9C%93&q=is%3Aissue++csp) seems like latter is the most likely case.

#6742 is a WIP to fix LDAP related test. #6084 needed a rebase. For team alerts (#6660), we need to come up with a character to mention teams. I was thinking of using `!` so that we use `!**support**`. Let me know what you think, @Steve Howell.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-28 16:29 UTC

Let's have a discussion about the character.  I think we do want it to lead with `@`, but might want to think a bit more about the syntax.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 16:37 UTC

Yeah, I think we should start it with `@` and have autocomplete mix teams and users, and somehow clearly call out teams vs. users.  (It should usually be obvious, but it's plausible to name teams after the human team lead, for lack of a better name for the team.)  One thought is `@!!support team!!`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-28 16:40 UTC

I'm not confident that users won't be happier with using the same syntax we use for user mentions.  I bet something like `@*support*` would be fine if we wanted to be as clean and similar as possible.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 16:46 UTC

I think we would regret having a syntax that boxes us into single-word team names.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 16:48 UTC

Hopefully most users use typeahead, so the syntax that we're debating is basically an implementation detail.  (I know it's sort of leaked to the user, but they don't have to actually type it.)  The backend value of having separate syntaxes is that it's easier on the render side to triage team mentions vs. user mentions, so you're not always checking both tables.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-28 17:09 UTC

Just added a code block around my proposal; it wouldn't box us into single-word.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 17:21 UTC

Cool, that's better.  I'd like something that more clearly disambiguates team from user, though, so we don't have to protect against team names like `*support*`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 17:22 UTC

It's also very close to `*italics*` (rendered as *italics*).

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-09-28 22:47 UTC

I think `@support` is what I would expect as a user.

Are we going to prevent team names from overlapping with user names?

**Umair Khan** · 2018-01-04 08:13 UTC

So I have still not been able to figure out why the 'process_queue' command fails to reload occasionally. The Django code responsible for reloading seems simple enough; it just loops through all the files and compares the 'modified times'. I have confirmed that the problem is not related to the logging code. One good thing is that I can reproduce the problem in my dev environment.

**Umair Khan** · 2018-01-05 08:25 UTC

About the process_queue reload test (#7961):

The autoreload code of Django works by looping over the files associated with all the loaded modules. This loop is run after every 1 second. If the file is found for the first time by the loop, it is assumed that the file is new and is not modified between the time it is loaded and is checked by the loop. This assumption is the source of a race condition. We can either implement a more sensitive version of the loop or we can just allow enough time to the Django loop to touch every file at least once. For the time being I have added some wait in the test to give loop some time to touch every file.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2018-01-16 15:45 UTC

Problem with Public/Private Key Crypto, is that there is a limit to the amount of data you can encrypt and send. If the key size is 4096-bit, you can only encrypt 4096 bits of data in one go, I guess you could split it into blocks and send it, but that's a lot of effort, or you could encrypt a AES key at the beginning, and encrypt the actual data with that random AES key.

Anyway, I think generating a new key for every new device is good enough.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2018-01-16 15:45 UTC

Because you'll be transporting that key over SSL while registering, so there shouldn't be any security issue either.

**Vishnu KS** · 2018-01-16 16:25 UTC

i don't actually think it is necessary to go to the extend of generating public/private keys pair for each mobile devices in this case. We would randomly generate a key when the user registers for the first time and it would be passed to the mobile device on registration or first login over HTTPS which takes care of distribution of the key securely. I can't think of any good reason why we should go to the extend of having a seperate public/private key for each device.

Right yeah, I was talking about symmetric key encryption as well, but I was thinking about the case where someone unregisters the device.

**Umair Khan** · 2018-02-13 09:07 UTC

#8047 now includes a new method to make Zulip dev work in Ubuntu 17.10. We will have to rely on this until we start using LXC 2.1.1 because in that version 'pivotdir' setting is ignored. The PR asks the users to follow a 2-step approach:
```
vagrant box add https://vagrantcloud.com/fgrehm/trusty64-lxc
vagrant up
```
In the first step, user is asked to download the box. Once the box is downloaded, we have access to the config file. In `vagrant up`, we update the file before creating the container.

So a detailed checkin from me has been long overdue.

I am also testing all of the integrations/webhooks and making sure that the screenshots are up to date and what not! @Rishi Gupta :smile: 

Also, I submitted #8423, making sure that every remaining fixture example in our `/api` docs is tested against a running server (except [`api/get-events-from-queue`](https://chat.zulip.org/api/get-events-from-queue) for reasons described [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zerver/lib/api_test_helpers.py#L416)). :tada: @Steve Howell, @Tim Abbott: FYI :smile: 

Next steps (these are not ordered by priority):

* Write a guide on how to add more API bindings and how to document them in a testable manner. This will also include documenting the Markdown extension for generating examples/fixtures.
* Write a "Getting started HOWTO" for our API in general, kind of like a first stop for anyone hoping to use our API.
* Improve the examples in the `zulip` API package and advertise them on the `api/` docs as standalone scripts. @Tim Abbott: I think you suggested this, right? :smile:
* Also, I will keep going through our webhook docs and updating them till everything is consistent and up-to-date.
* Also write a more detailed style guide on how to document a webhook/integration and what kind of language to use, what constitutes a separate step in the documentation, etc.

**Eeshan Garg** · 2018-11-20 18:16 UTC

@Vishnu Ks: Well because while Stripe has an amazing structure for testing their webhook, they have a couple of weird things going on in there:
* For "update" payloads such as `customer.subscription.update`, a host of smaller updates are grouped under the same payload with no indicators for which particular values were updated.
* Essentially, what Stripe's API does is lazily give you a `previous_attributes` object in the JSON that you have to manually diff with the new attributes of the payload to figure out what was changed. This is absolutely terrible, if something is updated, an API should do the legwork for figuring out what exactly was changed and only send me the relevant attributes. Another thing to get around that is to just have more "sub-events".
* For instance, a structure where a `changes` object had a list of attributes with a `[attribute: {old: 'old_value', new: 'new_value'},]` sorta structure would have been much much better!

Having said that, I really do admire their work on the documentation and the testing system, so they aren't too bad, and Atlassian is much worse!

**Vishnu KS** · 2018-11-20 18:59 UTC

hmm. That sounds bad.

**Eeshan Garg** · 2018-11-20 19:38 UTC

@Vishnu Ks: Its bad in a few ways rather than one. If they followed the structure I suggested, they could trim down the number of event types by a lot!

**Vishnu KS** · 2018-11-20 19:58 UTC

I wonder why they went like that. They are really focused on developer productivity and happiness. Maybe try emailing them? We should be able to get more details on the design decisions.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-11-20 20:00 UTC

well, I think their webhook system is designed for building a billing system, rather than for chat updates

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-11-20 20:01 UTC

e.g. they don't include the information necessary to make a good webhook integration, like the customer name or other human-readable elements

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-11-20 20:03 UTC

my guess is they didn't have anything like slack or zulip in mind at all when they were designing it :)

**Eeshan Garg** · 2018-11-20 20:14 UTC

Yeah, that makes sense, which is why I am not too too mad. Its a lot more annoying when a productivity company like Atlassian makes these mistakes.

**Eeshan Garg** · 2018-11-20 20:15 UTC

I have to say though, still, Stripe is pretty amazing. I know people who have worked there and they have very good things to say about the company!

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-11-20 20:28 UTC

though I should say I also agree that it seems uncharacteristic of them to not include the old and new values here, or e.g. {old, new, url-to-resource}

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-27 00:58 UTC

> This is random, but has anyone experienced sharp pain in one of their wrists (pain that extends to the hand's knuckles) due to prolonged typing? I have been spending a lot of time typing these last few weeks (10 hours a day?), and I can't type without feeling a tinge of pain in my dominant hand.

Yes.  In fact, most programmers I know developed some sort of wrist pain either during college or soon after.  "RSI" is the term for it.  Pushing through the pain is generally ill-advised -- I have friends who had to stop typing for a year because they ignored this sort of pain while addicted to a computer game.  

This manifests for different folks differently, as Rishi said.  For me, it started my last year in college and was bad enough that I couldn't use a computer for more than ~20 minutes at a time without pain, and dropped the one class left in my CS major (I had math+physics already), and was pretty annoying to debug, since it the pain had a lag like 24 hours from when I spent too much time using a computer nonergonomically.  I was able to solve my RSI issues completely by (1) never use a laptop screen except for brief events like sprints, preferring a proper ergonomic setup with a real monitor properly aligned at eye level and (2) starting a weight-lifting exercise routine.  

So be careful!

**Rhea Parekh** · 2018-02-01 12:28 UTC

updates:

Finished with #8123, being my biggest PR till now:sweat_smile:

It covers:
1. Refactoring the slack import script to break it into smaller functions for testing and understanding convenience.
2. Thorough unit tests for all functions except `do_convert_data` covering the border cases and all foreign key relations.
3. One minor test for message conversion in `/tests/test_slack_message_conversion`
4. We faced the issue of the email data of users missing in the dataset we get from slack export (tested on fresh exports of various different slack organisation data). But, in the older method of getting slack data (using legacy token), the emails are still included in the user data. So I implemented the new method of fetching this data ( a get request to the slack users api with the token) and added tests for the same.
5. Checked in a sample dataset zip file in `/fixtures` and updated the` /tools/test-slack-importer` to use this dataset and see the working of importing a converted slack to zulip data file into an existing non-empty db.

* FineUploader: https://fineuploader.com/index.html
* Dropzone.js: http://www.dropzonejs.com/

Both supports chunked uploads. And as mentioned in an [old conversation](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/9-issues/topic/MAX_FILE_UPLOAD_SIZE) to make chunked upload happening we may need to work on backend also.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-05-25 07:33 UTC

So I looked around and it feels to me like fineuploader would be a better choice. (I reached the same conclusion when I was looking into possible upload lib sometime ago though at the time I didn't know about dropzone.js)
Basically it has lots of features (progress bars, chunked uploads and others). We will probably have a better luck reusing this project as a backend lib (https://pypi.org/project/django-fine-uploader/) rather than what's out there for the dropzone.js. The backend available for fineuploader seems much more useful than what's available for the dropzone.js

So I think we should go ahead with fineuploader. thoughts?

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-05-25 08:04 UTC

If we are gonna do this I think we should first try to use the django-fine-uploader package as it is by including in the app and see how things play out with it. Basically what we can do is to try setup a prototype to see how well it works. Doing it with just using the pypi package should be easy, basically adding  new lib and configure backend according to settings in the instructions should be all we need to do on backend front and for the front end we will probably do the same drill that is add fineuploader to our yarn deps, serve the node module using webpack. Since we have been using Jquery I guess it might make sense to use the jquery plugin which fineuploader offers which is just a wrapper around fine uploader.

I was trying to access our localhost in mobile for investigating some unusual behavior of mobile web app on chrome. Here are my efforts for this:
* Tried following [this simple answer at stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4779963/how-can-i-access-my-localhost-from-my-android-device) but this works for a simple server like Apache but not for vagrant port forwarded Django server.  

* Tried using `ngrok` for making localhost:9991 accessible via a public URL but this worked only for portico pages as I'm unable to authenticate in dev login page because requests are sent to `localhost` by `information` and since these URLs are generated by Django, so yet I've to figure out how to make this working as I don't know that I've to tweak Django settings or configurations of vagrant or ngrok.   
* Then I found a magical vagrant command `vagrant share` but this does the same thing as above i.e. it also makes HTTP port publically accessible by `ngrok`, so faced the same problem.

**Tommy Ip** · 2019-06-11 12:27 UTC

Today I started working on reducing our webpack build time in development mode. Profiling shows that most of the build time is spent bundling all the modules and in sass-loader (transpiling scss to css).

* I have some success using hard-source-webpack-plugin to cache all the computation that webpack performs but rarely changes across builds (we do use cache-loader but that only caches the result of our loaders): build time with cold cache ~8 sec vs with warm cache after server restart (not hot reload) ~2.5 sec. At the moment I couldn't figure out a way for it to not interfere with all the files file-loader handles, which is causing file not found errors.
* Another method to reduce build time is to extract out all the third party modules and build them separately (only when adding/removing libraries) from our app bundle. I am trying to use webpack's built-in DllPlugin to achieve this though our "export everything to global" approach doesn't play nicely with it.

**Priyank Patel** · 2019-06-11 15:04 UTC

For, the sass-loader issue, I looked into `fast-scss-loader` the only problem with using that would be if we have same variable name across files it would cause issues since that plugin munges all the files into one and compiles them. sass-loader is slow because it calls native bindings for sass library for every single file.

About the exporting everything to global, I think its worth discussing using `import` when/after we do typescript migration. One issue with doing that would be we might want zulip related modules (`message`, `narrow` and friends) to be available from console, I think we can do that by exporting those to `window`  or `window.zulip`

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-12 01:44 UTC

Turns out my approach is similar to the one describe here https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/10018#issuecomment-407329911 using proxyquire. But this is very fragile when testing a module that holds states at the top level, example:
```js
// node_tests/composebox_typeahead.js
...
zrequire('people');
zrequire('composebox_typeahead');
set_global('md5', function (s) {
   return 'md5-' + s;
}
...
// Change some states in people
people.add_in_realm(hamlet);
...
people.get_person_from_user_id = function (user_id) {
    var users = {100: hamlet, 104: lear};
    return users[user_id];
};
people.my_current_email = function () {
    return 'hamlet@zulip.com';
};
...
// Do some more testing
```
people is converted to a typescript module, and all the modules (ie composebox_typeahead) that need it `require` it instead of using `window.people`. In this test, we are mocking md5 which is a dependency of people, we also mock some functions in people. People holds a few dicts at the top level.

To make the mock works in the test we do something like
```js
const people = proxyquire('people', {
    'blueimp-md5': function (s) {
        return 'md5-' + s;
    }
});
const people_stub = {};
proxyquire('composebox_typeahead', {
    'people': people_stub
});
...
people.add_in_realm(hamlet);
...
people_stub.get_person_from_user_id = function (user_id) {
    var users = {100: hamlet, 104: lear};
    return users[user_id];
};
people_stub.my_current_email = function () {
    return 'hamlet@zulip.com';
};
...
```
The problem is the `proxyquire('people')`in the test does not return the same instance as the `require('people')`inside composebox_typeahead, so calling `people.add_in_realm(hamlet);` in the test won't affect the state of people in composebox_typeahead.

**Priyank Patel** · 2018-01-31 17:46 UTC

Hey guys.

I think we can add cloud9 as an option in docs for developing remotely. There were some issue running zulip dev server and provision on cloud9 but i got it fixed and also created a npm package for it called zulip-cloud9 which takes care of it. 

The problems running dev server on cloud9 were the services were not running (rabbitmq-server, memcached, redis-server and postgresql) and in `tools/run-dev.py` the port web_proxy port needed to be changed to `8080` and instead `127.0.0.1` had to change it to 0.0.0.0. This is where zulip-cloud9 comes in to rescue. I documented errors in detail at https://github.com/cPhost/zulip-cloud9/wiki/Errors.

It start all required services if needed and then runs `run-dev.py` script which is modifed for c9 needs so as a user they don't have to modify anything.  

So to start a dev-server on cloud9 they just have to run `zulip-dev start`.  Any guidance for adding this to docs or any feedback would be appreciated.

## Satyendra

*2018-02-05 to 2018-02-05 · 1 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/65-checkins/topic/Satyendra/with/481849)*

**satyendra banjare** · 2018-02-05 02:12 UTC

Hello Every One, I am very excited to share with you all that I finally got  the searching your messages for mentioned users (as mentioned in issue [#6902](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/6902)) working. :smile: 

 PR - [#8266]( https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/8266) 

a quick video of this feature in working is given here: [updated_search_feature.mp4](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/bd/XkA6keJIsI4XeibIh9Jjdg-7/updated_search_feature.mp4) 

There are some extra suggestions provided when you start searching with '@' which are suggested out of currently narrowed messages. The suggestions then take you to that particular suggested message. The problem of message having @<username> styling has also been taken care of and `@My_UserName` is simply displayed as "@My_UserName " in suggestion description as can be seen in above video.

As displayed above the rendered mentioned message suggestions include :
**<**Date when conversation took place**> **  **<**a small description of message string (26 characters long as of now)**> **  and the **<**mentioned user name and email id**>**.

The `current_msg_list` is filtered using the ids only to check if user is present.The ids here include `sender_id`, `message_id` and the `to_be_checked_user_id` and if message's data-user-id[]  includes the to_be_checked_user_id and sender_id is equal to user_id ,  the message is suggested. 

There a couple of adjustments required.:
* As of now this method is unable to search when you are narrowed to a private-message with a particular user. 
* Also this search fails as of now when mentioned user is searched in a particular topic messages of a stream.


While working on this, these are couple of things I understood.

* The `zerver/lib/message.py` checks and string matches the` @__ `pattern and return a list of **user_names_list**.
* The `Bugdown/__init__.py/MentionData` then uses this function to get a list of mentioned user_names. It then generate a users_info_dict() out of those **user_names_list** whose contents are user_id , user_email etc which is then used while creating messages in database as in `do_send_messages` function of `zerver/actions.py`to finally create message data .
* Since the `Bugdown/__init__.py/MentionData` method starts generating user_info_dict() using only user_names, it instantly feeds the *first user's information* whose name matches the **user_names_list** values and feeds only that to users_info_dict(). 
I think this is the root cause of mentioning same named user issues and the issue [#374](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/374). 

As pointed by @Rishi Gupta  in here [link](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/issues/subject/same.20name.20users.20wrongly.20mentioned/near/470362). We can reconstruct the mentioned user name as @NAME(id) and then get user's id from mention.py and then proceed with creating `users_info_dict()` using **ids** and **not names**.

pinging @Rishi Gupta  @Tim Abbott  @Steve Howell 

next I plan to do is to write tests and update this PR.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2018-05-19 04:37 UTC

> We are facing some problems setting up the dev environment, I will try and fix it today.
@Aman Agrawal I spent some time working on this, this morning.  And it looks like adding an additional step of running `python setup.py develop` at the end of the dev setup instructions is the best way to go about this. 

`pipenv` comes with an option to install an editable package, and we could replace the `pipenv install --dev` command with `pipenv install "-e ."`, but that changes the `Pipfile` and adds the `zulipterminal` repo at the current commit as a dependency. This would be a problem to maintain. But, it looks like the command is just doing whatever `pipenv install --dev` does + whatever `python setup.py develop` would do.  

I can send a PR to fix this.

Even just learning the alphabet is pretty great; I found early on that it let me read Russian names when written in cyrillic.

**Rein Zustand** · 2020-07-07 02:50 UTC

There is a theory of language acquisition that uses a technique called comprehensible input (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Input_hypothesis), which is meant to emulate how a baby learn a language. A way to do the learning is by watching a video where the meaning of the audio input can be understood from the pictures. Can the words in Sesame Street be understood just from the context of the visual input?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-07 02:52 UTC

I think Sesame Street builds on top of natural language acquisition, and it teaches things like the alphabet and reading that aren't necessarily as intrinsic to humans as speaking, but which are certainly practical.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-07 02:52 UTC

(but I don't really know)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-11 23:09 UTC

Lily continues to pretend play with everyone assigned an animal identity each day, whether a polar bear or moose or sea lion or whatever (sometimes an identity lasts a few days). **Tim Abbott** · 2020-11-26 17:06 UTC

Lily has been doing all sorts of exciting new things over the last few months.  A few I'll mention today are:
* Reading by herself!  She's now read about 6 books from a collection of 8 tiny Russian language books, each with about 20 words (12 distinct) across 12 pages.  It's very exciting to see her doing this sort of thing.
* Learning English!  We've been doing Kinderlingo (Duolingo's kids thing) for 10 minutes every few days and she's actually learned like 30 words, finally.
* Reading digital clocks!  Lily really likes to say what time it is, and then discuss when it's going to be the next minute until ... it's arrived!  It's extremely good for her practicing her 2-digits numbers. (She can count 25+ objects at this point, or "how many arms do the monkeys on this page have", where she remembers to count the ones that are not visible in the picture).
* The most exciting is that we now have a beach a 25-minute walk from our home.  Yes, it's a new development, and we didn't move!  SF opened a park with a large sandy beach just each of USCF, replacing an old warehouse/pier area.  I can't express how amazing it feels to have a new beach be built nearby.

The giraffe needs diaper changes (sometimes at inconvenient times), fusses when it's hungry or tired, is strolled to sleep for naps and swaddled for bed time, etc.

Yes, this is from the GCI Summit. That's @skunkmb (Marco Burstein) giving a lightening talk about his GCI experience.

**skunkmb (Marco Burstein)** · 2018-06-28 13:02 UTC

Yep, that's me! It was great getting a chance to talk about what working with Zulip was like for me and to say thank you to the Zulip mentors and community. Thanks for the picture, @Rohitt Vashishtha.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-01 09:46 UTC

@skunkmb (Marco Burstein) awesome!  I'd love to hear any thoughts on your experience at the GCI summit :)

**skunkmb (Marco Burstein)** · 2018-07-03 03:46 UTC

@Tim Abbott It was fantastic! It was great meeting @Rohitt Vashishtha in-person since he was such a helpful mentor to me. Rohitt really helped make my Zulip experience special, and I’m so glad that I chose Zulip because of how welcoming the mentors have been. It was also incredible being at the Google campus, and I feel so appreciative that I had the chance to see the inner-workings of such an amazing company!

While at Google, we got to see lots of presentations about open-source technology as well as Google’s current projects. One of my favorites was the one about the legal side of open-source, including the specifics of different license types, what your rights are as an open source contributor, and more. I also really enjoyed a talk that we heard about Google's various platforms (Android, ChromeOS, and Fuchsia) and how they both intersect and are distinct from one another.

I had the opportunity to give a brief talk about my own experience working with Zulip, as well, which I really enjoyed. It was nice getting a chance to introduce the other winners to Zulip and why it’s so useful. One of the OSPO directors, Josh, actually reached out to me about turning that presentation into a blog post for the Google Open Source blog, which I’m super excited about! When it’s posted, I can send you the link if you’re interested.

As soon as I got back home from the GCI trip, I actually headed back out with my family on a two-week road trip. During the trip, I won’t be able to be very active here at Zulip, but when I get back I’ll have lots of time to contribute.

Thanks again for choosing me as a GCI winner! I hope you’re having a great summer!

 - #10314: uploads: Create a placeholder when uploading.

Even I found it quite hard to reset my laptop the first time. I recently reset it (for like the 3rd time since I bought) and this time the experience was quite smooth. I have written an install script that starts with `brew` and builds it way upto everything I need (mostly) on my mac. The script lies on a repo on my Github account along with the `.zshrc` and VSCode settings.

**One of the biggest mistake that I made was not have a backup of my SSH keys.** Just mentioning, if someone hasn't they really should.

I don't keep any photos or anything heavy on my laptop, everything's on either Google Drive or external storage hence it might be even easier for me to get my laptop in the same state as before.

Last weekend, I have created bot named **botlatexx** (not actually a bot, but helps in generating pdf from latex files and pushes back generated pdf to GitHub).
Here is a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P_5-_v2ttiU&t=2s
Github: [@botlatexx](https://github.com/botlatexx)
Twitter: [@botlatexx](https://twitter/botlatexx)
Webpage: https://botlatexx.github.io


If you push your latex code to Github repo, then it's PDF file will also be present in the repo. BotLatexx is a bot which keep tracks of your pushes and generate PDF whenever code get changed. It saves time in manually setting up local latex environment and your precious memory (MacTex is ~3.0 GB). :)

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-17 23:41 UTC

Hmm. I've never actually read the "Gang of Four" book, but the discussion I read about it in the early '00s seemed pretty convincing to me at the time that it was already quite dated then.

Wikipedia summarizes pretty well the criticisms I have in mind:

> A primary criticism of Design Patterns is that its patterns are simply workarounds for missing features in C++, replacing elegant abstract features with lengthy concrete patterns, essentially becoming a "human compiler" or "generating by hand the expansions of some macro".[4] Peter Norvig demonstrates that 16 out of the 23 patterns in Design Patterns are simplified or eliminated (via direct language support) in Lisp or Dylan.[5] 

The references are [here](http://www.norvig.com/design-patterns/design-patterns.pdf) for Norvig... and the other one is by an author who's now better-known for other work:
http://www.paulgraham.com/icad.html

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-17 23:44 UTC

(And that's C++ of the mid-'90s -- I think in modern C++ today you'd have basically the abstractions you'd want from Lisp back then. Similarly in Python, which was much less prominent then.)

**Yash RE** · 2020-04-18 05:37 UTC

I *REALLY* wish people in my university took the subject ISOE532C more seriously. Everyone. Students, faculty, Teaching assistants.
It's an IT department course, titled Software engineering, 5th sem course, 3 theory credits and 2 lab credits, a core (compulsory) course.


Everyone in my college saw it as a "management" course, and of course the perception that "management" is distinct from "real engineering"  meant that no one even bothered to pay attention. It was shared by two faculties. One which treated the course with such respect, and tried really hard to share concepts with us. The other, who didn't even bother to read their own slides and would just flip through them (kinda because none of the other students wanted to study anyway).

But, honestly? It was one of the most fascinating subjects for me... And a big part of the reason why I gave it a lot of respect was because I'd had the opportunity to see first hand (through Zulip) a lot of the things which were being spoken about. Here's a simple example:

Our professor introduced [SDLC umbrella activities](https://www.c-sharpcorner.com/UploadFile/nipuntomar/computer-aided-software-engineering-tools-case/Images/CaseTools2.gif).

No one was paying attention.
Our professor was disheartened.
He said: "Let me explain why we're studying this, for example, what do you think would be the consequences of a mistake during the requirement analysis phase?"
No answer for a while, then someone said: "The final product will be wrong."
He said: "Right, and the whole cycle will need to be implemented again and that will raise the time and monetary costs of development, alright, now, what do you think would be the consequences of a mistake during the modeling (design) phase?"
No answered for a while then someone repeated the previous answer.
He said: "Wrong. While it's possible that the produced software may be functional and satisfy client needs, the team will face major challenges during the *testing* (verification) phase, because your tests will not align with reality, and as a result the software will be buggy and of low quality, and that in turn will raise the time and monetary costs of development."

The whole class barely heard what he said, meanwhile, I was sitting in the corner *shaking*.
If I had some more time I'd go to him and speak a little about project ideas I have.... maybe I still can, once the pandemic dies down :thinking:.
