**Yash RE** · 2021-12-04 10:56 UTC

A couple of notes:
1. At the start of this month I came to the conclusion that I should not send in PRs late at night, or at least, not promote/consider them ready for review:
The motivations behind sending something in at night / near the end of the day are fairly simple:
(a) There's a good chance they'd get feedback by the next morning, so I'd have something concrete to start the day's work with.
(b) I'd have a neat time frame for when I want a piece of work to be done by.
However, the issues this practice would cause are:
(i) It would encourage me to rush things eg favor short term fixes, not do a good read through post PR creation, etc
(ii) Even on things that are getting double checked, it would still encourage mistakes coming through just because of being tired / less sharp and unable to spot things... Typos / poor grammar in commit messages being the most common example.

2.  I feel like I could have done more this month, but I think I might have had a little less focus, since some had gone towards implementing lifestyle changes, 2 or 3 weeks ago, I freaked out a little after noticing how much my weight had risen... Starting exercise has involved a decent amount of learning through experience, key things being:
(a) Exercising late at night is quite liable to prevent a good nights sleep, and having one sleepless night can lead to an entire week of disturbed sleep cycles.
(b) Doing a lot of jump rope on a hard floor such as concrete or ceramic is a fantastic way of getting shin splints and pain around the achilles tendon.
(c) Managing meal portions and timings is an important part of getting results.
(d) Any intense routine needs to have recovery days.
I'm finally approaching a stable state where I only need to spend between 20 to 45 minutes a day on exercise, but I'm creating a calorie deficit.
I'm considering getting a treadmill, and using it as a walking desk for around an hour a day, but I haven't made the investment yet. Still, I think the change from wontfix to wip is significant.

3. I had an interesting thought recently... I wonder if I/we could set goals along the lines of "improve test coverage by 0.01% everyday"... it doesn't have to be 0.01%,  it doesn't have to be everyday, it could be 0.1%, it could be every week. I'm just curious if such goals can be made and realistically worked towards.

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2019-02-28 19:47 UTC

Hello everyone, I thought that I'd start writing some updates occasionally on what I'm up to, so here goes  :slight_smile: 

Currently I'm working on writing an integration (incoming webhook) for BitBucket Server.

- The first step was to read up on all the literature that Zulip has on webhooks, read some of the source code for some important classes and methods used here,  and skim through the code for existing webhooks to get familiar with the common patterns involved in this field. I completed that about 2 days ago.

- The next step was to get an instance of bitbucket server up and running so that I can begin experimenting with it. While I'm not done with this step yet, I've made some fair progress. Here's how my ***adventure***'s been so far (I hope that anyone reading this might be able to learn something or the other from my experience):

1. In order to get bitbucket server one would have to make a bitbucket account and then they'd be able to get a 30-day free trial (students seem to get some additional perks, but I haven't done too much investigation into what they exactly are - free private repos  are one of them I think). Then we could download a tar file for it (~290 mb). But for some reason,  the internet here at my university has been pretty slow for the past two days.... so after an agonizing hour and a half I finally got it to download.

2. Get a server and get this tar file on there. Luckily, I already had a server (DO Droplet) running for another project I'm working on (the backend for an mini-ewallet + show tickets manager for my university's upcoming tech fest - this is a development server of course). So I decided to go ahead and set up bitbucket server there. Used SFTP and uploaded the tar file I downloaded (because there is no direct link to curl bitbucket server from - at least as far as I know)... So that was another hourish (less than an hour though).

here's where the fun part actually starts
3.  BitBucket server uses Java, and that means that it's pretty memory hungry... So I just couldn't get it to run the installer on the small server I have :sweat_smile: . I originally planned to upgrade my server (because why not) however I decided to get a little hacky... I realized that my secondary space requirements were not too much, and the *beautiful* thing with Linux systems is that you can set up a ***swap space***, so that's exactly what I did... memory problems solved :thumbs_up: 

4. BitBucket server requires that you complete the installation procedure via. a browser on localhost:7990..... and I'm trying to install it on a remote VPS..... at first I was kinda stumped and I tried to see if I could modify some of the source files to change this but to no avail. So a bit of googling and I stumbled across [this](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/33764038/access-localhost-port-remotely/33764165) beautiful link and learnt about something called **SSH Port Tunneling** (Something new I learnt today :smiley: )

5. Now after getting BitBucket Server running and after connecting via. SSH Port Tunneling, it complained that my version of Git was outdated and that I should upgrade. So after adding PPA keys for the repo and updating to the latest version, I was greeted by a beautiful message telling me that the version was too advanced and that I have to downgrade git :shrug: I decided to download the exact version that they suggested: 2.11.0 but here's the catch: I couldn't get it via. the apt manager. So then I had to get"off-road" - I used git to clone git from github and then used git to revert this cloned version of git to the right version and replace git with git... git! Now the tricky part was building from source.... and it wasn't a straightforward path since *several header* files and packages required were missing but let me just say that there is no greater feeling than saying that you "built something from source". Here's a word of advice for newcomers to this... if you're missing some header files, you should just find the package to apt install to get them instead of trying to get those from source too. There's almost always a package for them, find it.

6. Now continuing the installation, I have to connect bitbucket server to the a database but the catch is that they discourage MySQL, and SQL Server required 2 GB of RAM to run (which is twice my max capacity), ruling out the 2 DBs that I'm comfortable with... that leaves me with PostgreSQL or Oracle both of which are new to me. Another adventure for tomorrow :smile: 

And that's what happened today..... This checkin ended up becoming **much** longer than I originally intended, guess I'll have to cut down on what I talk about next time :sweat_smile:  Let me know if you gained anything useful from my experience today so I know what to include and what not to include in my next checkin.

- Started working on an incoming webhook style integration for Launchpad only to realize that it's still in a beta phase and that it wouldn't be of much use to us yet (certain important events are not yet supported). So I had to abandon this. But one thing that I need to mention was that the folks over at Launchpad were pretty great in providing me assistance with generating test fixtures for this.

- A Phabricator webhook style integration.  We're temporary holding off on further development of this since there are a good number of pre-req that need to be carefully designed and put into place before this.

- Some miscellaneous documentation related changes (One thing I've realized since getting into open source is that documentation is really important since even if you make a great feature, unless it's well documented most people won't ever use it and those that do might get confused and thus frustrated). PR #12482 and PR #12481 are currently open, waiting on a bit more review here.

-  I started work on making a UI that will allow to users to configure their incoming webhook type bots (there's a BotConfigData model on the backend side which would allow us to store key-value pairs for bot configuration purposes). This is a pre-req to the Phabricator webhook style integration. This has also been blocked since we might be introducing a new system for this before create a UI to accompany it (it would most likely parallel the current system that we have in place for embedded bots). Luckily one of the commits could be perhaps be merged soon (though there's no rush here, in fact it might be better to wait before merging anything).

- A new system for being able to store HTTP headers for any integration that requires them for testing purposes. Currently in discussion with @Eeshan Garg and @Tim Abbott about how we could make the system as great as we can :slight_smile: . It's PR #12515 in case anyone wants to check out the technical design discussion.

- Submitted a small PR for fixing a small bug in the `parse_headers` method found in `zerver/management/commands/send_webhook_fixture_message.py`. I originally forgot to account for the fact that Django does not "Djangoify" the "Content-Type" and "Content-Length" headers.

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2019-06-24 19:56 UTC

This week I got a little distracted (mainly with the Google CTF 2019 Beginner's Quest and a couple of other small things and issues that popped up) but otherwise, here's what I was able to do:

- Continued work on the HTTP fixtures system. We finally merged PR #12515 and to polish up the system (follow ups) I opened up PR #12622 , ready for review.
- I continued my work on issue #10907 - this issue aims to introduce a general/common framework for our integrations to perform a HTTP callback to a third party API, which we'd need if the webhook payload doesn't contain enough data (usually, this happens if the payload contains references to data instead of the actual data) . After changing my mindset towards the issue (which was a major blocking factor), I completely revamped/changed my approach. I think that the system I've designed might be a *little* overkill, but I'm pretty happy with the design as it allows us to have a powerful general system which can be **greatly** tweaked/customized according to the needs of the endpoint (authentication, number of requests, need to notify the user of a reconfigured bot, etc.).
- Now regarding the system/framework (not sure what to call it) mentioned above, I'm working on the Phabricator integration as a functional proof of concept. The thing is that while working on this new complexities keep popping up. For example, I realized I needed make my "simple token auth handler" function more general purpose, and also now that we require that users have to configure their bots (api keys and whatnot), we need to catch mis-configurations in a systematic way and then notify the user about it (also, the design for this is pending as mentioned in my previous checkin). So a lot of different things are coming together all at once. Also, I'm going to need to create an good set of tests for all of this as well as document the new system in an easy to understand and friendly manner.

So for this week, I plan on completing the Phabricator integration,  polishing, testing and documenting the new system, thus issue #10907. With my focus returning to Zulip, it should definitely be a possible goal.

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2019-08-01 05:00 UTC

This week marks the end of my summer vacation and the start of a new semester and academic year.  I've spent the past few days spending time with family, shopping for some thing I need to take to college, packing, travelling, discussing with my friends and seniors about which courses to take, getting my timetable ready, setting up my room, etc. so I haven't been able to contribute much these past 4 days. But now that most of the hassle seems to be over, I'm ready to jump right back in.

Here's some of the bigger things that I have been/am working on:

- Added a few important changes to the OpenAPI Validation test suite. The most important change being adding some 3-5 lines that made the tests compatible with Python 3.5 (and thus allowed PR #12751 to get merged).

- We've recently discovered that some of our cURL examples in the documentation are incorrect (e.g. trying to send GET parameters as POST parameters). So I did a quick manual audit to fix these and now I'm following up by creating a few functions that will allow us to automatically generate these examples by using the OpenAPI documentation (I'll be translating this to a template tag and a test or two soon after). This way we can avoid human errors and having to do extra work (the current system is that the cURL example would have to be manually written).

- I haven't gotten very far on it yet, but soon we'll be adding production support to Debian Buster (Debian 10). Most of the work around here has to do with Postgresql - Zulip uses some special libraries/extentions like tsearch_extras and pgroonga and we have to make sure that they work well with (or are adapted for) Postgresql 11. There are probably other big quirks hiding beyond Postgresql too, but it seems like this will be a great learning experience and I'm looking forward to it! (I just have to take care of some other things first).

`777M	./postgresql/`
going all the way up to (!):
`(zulip-py3-venv) vagrant@ubuntu-bionic:/var/lib$ sudo du -sh ./postgresql/`

  * As such, I'll be focusing on #12426, along with investigating other memory leak issues.

* I had PR #12458 merged regarding caching the migrations files (although, this is going to need some followup work regarding removing `var/test_db_status/postgres_init_test_db`, but research needs to be done for adding code to get the uuid in the Shell.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-02 18:42 UTC

My main advice here is to get one that's comfortable on your eyes; you're realistically going to spend a ton of hours looking at said monitor every single week.  This advice is more extreme for keyboards and mice; basically one can ignore price when buying those because they last a long time and they're very inexpensive compared to every other aspect of a computer, so just find the best one for you.  

(It can vary by person what that means -- I am still using the 2 copies I have of a keyboard that I bought in ~2009 that I find comfortable, I think because the curve on it is a good fit for the distance between my shoulders / hand size or something; newer models from the same brand and model line feel worse to me).

**Kanishk Kakar** · 2019-06-13 15:57 UTC

Checking in after a while, and there's a fair bit of stuff I've been working on:

Desktop app:

1. Adding spellchecker options - #D752 - addresses user suggestions to add app-side overrides to the spellchecker language. This PR adds 3 options for spellcheck in the app: automatically detect language being used for input (default), use the org-level language and switch correspondingly, and a hard override that is used across the entire app. 

2. Enterprise config - #D681 - allows admins to create a config `.json` file in an admin-only write folder and makes app read the user settings and preset orgs. Also adds options for settings and orgs to be `isAdminOnly` - when they cannot override an admin-defined setting. We should be able to merge the preset orgs portion by this weekend, and then we'll discuss the UI changes involved with the user settings portion. 

3. Updating server validation logic - #D750 (merged) - removes the outdated `.ogg` file check flow and replaces that with the `v1` server settings API. Also refactors code to use `async await` instead of `then` chaining. 

4. Auto update testing and doc changes - #D746, #12373, #12358 (all merged) - helped Akash with testing out the broken autoupdate feature on Windows, the change of the GitHub URL and the corresponding updates to our documentation. 

5. Add option to find accounts by email - #D745 (merged) - adds our `/find/accounts` option to the desktop app and opens the relevant link in the browser.

6. Add custom `zulip://` URI scheme - #D716 (WIP) - one of my more challenging PRs, this is somewhat tricky to get right on Windows and Linux. Been working on some issues regarding redirection with Akash. Will update everyone with the progress here.

Documentation:

1. Remote dev with `rmate` - #12421 - Adds instructions to our remote dev docs for developing with `rmate`. Uses VS Code as an example code editor. 
2. Remote dev with PyCharm - #12534 - Adds instructions to our remote dev docs for developing over SSH with PyCharm Professional. I think that these instructions do away with the somewhat redundant steps in the JetBrains docs.

**Kanishk Kakar** · 2019-06-13 15:58 UTC

I'll be doing weekly check-ins from now on. Definitely a habit worth sticking to.

**Kanishk Kakar** · 2019-06-23 19:15 UTC

Updates from last week:

1. #D752 finalized and approved, waiting for merge. This PR now defaults to spellchecking the language the user is _typing in_, using the server language as context for initialization. Feedback wrt this feature's performance (our major concern) has been very positive so far. 
2. #D681 finalized and approved, waiting for supporting review and merge. This is a simplified version for the features I mentioned last week, so admins should now find it easier to write up configs. 
3. #D674 merged. Adds a loading indicator to the sidebar to remove confusion during login, so users know the app isn't inactive. (Works similar to a browser).
4. #D761 merged. Fixes a frequently occurring error in the main process with our database. 
5. #D714 reviewed again and discussed - this should fix a recurring problem with our server icons in the sidebar defaulting to the character icon even though a real server icon is present.
6. #D750 - went through this PR again in light of the feedback I got from #D752. After #D761 was merged, the PR works well for me, I'm trying to figure out where to reduce disk reads and writes so similar errors with our `settings.json` don't pop up. 
7.  #D617 - waiting for review on long-standing feature request that allows sidebar icons to be dragged around.

**Kanishk Kakar** · 2019-07-08 17:49 UTC

Been a while. Lost track of time, sorry!

Updates since I last posted:

1. #D730 reviewed, discussed, and reworked - adds translations to the app menus and all settings pages. Was earlier written to change locale on tab switch and then was changed to simply use the system locale after discussing this further with the community. 
2. #D781 prepared and put on hold - involves a leap upgrade to Electron v5. Since we're currently on v3 and this would be a big change, I wrote up a list of breaking changes that we should be concerned about and useful new APIs for simplifying our code. Put on hold because this update will also involve changes to electron-builder and electron-updater that could break autoupdate if not tested carefully.
3. #D617 completed and tested - makes org tabs draggable in sidebar. A useful new UI feature, it treats server tabs the same way as browser tabs, such that they can be dragged according to the user's preference. It's confused me for quite a while, so  I was glad to finally see this finished. (pending review)
4. #D752 finalized and merged. (Adds spellchecker for auto-detect). 
5. Writing a database wrapper for `leveldb` - we have plans to change our JSON database soon to one with proper locking and errors on concurrent access by different processes (we've chosen Google's `leveldb`). I've written up a basic wrapper for common database operations. 

Reviewed #D752. This PR converts the codebase to TypeScript, so we figured it was best to pause work on `async-await` migration till this was merged and the problems sorted out. We should be able to pick up pace after tonight. :)

Hi guys! It's been a while since I actively started contributing to Zulip, so I thought of writing down my journey. Each issue I picked up and worked on introduced me to many new concepts and tricks. A little bit of history of what I have learnt so far :sweat_smile: 

- The first issue I worked on was #13139 which involved handling large stream names. I learnt a lot about Zulip's work ethics and commit/PR style. Made my first PR #13250 for this, adding ellipsis to cut-short names, which got merged few weeks ago. 
-While working on the above issue, @Yash RE  noticed that the [view stream button](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/13250/commits/afbf6a56d24407c8d6fc754fcdda2fef1516ab71) was broken in master, so he helped me out in mending it. (Thanks man!)
-The first major issue I worked on was changing the warning message for wildcard mentions #13636. I was unaware of regex patterns, which were being used to catch the wildcard mentions, so @Vinit Singh  helped me out with figuring it out. However, due to limitations of regex functions in JS, I had to do some hacky code for the right wildcard mention to be displayed in the warning. Nonetheless, #13705 got merged closing this issue. Also, got to know how changes need to be done in the test suites for each change in the codebase. The extensive tests are another feature of the Zulip project that intrigues me.

All of this wrapped up by the beginning of this month, after which I got busy with a hackathon I participated in, Hack36 at NIT Allahabad. My team made a product for ADHD patients to keep track of their growth ([check it out here](https://github.com/vaibhavrajsingh2001/all_kavs36). Also had exams during this time, due to which I could contribute much.

Current work:

-The PR for long stream names (#13250) needed some edits for proper editing of long stream names for which I made #13995 . Sorry, @Tim Abbott for the delay on these edits. This is a sort of test PR, so more edits are incoming.
-Looking forward to continue Tim's work on #13274 .

**Divyanshu Agrawal** · 2020-03-30 17:59 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-30 18:00 UTC

An anecdote I remember from that, in phonology specifically, is that for many years the newsletter of a major professional association of phonologists was... written in IPA.

That is, people would write in English, but instead of normal English spelling with the Latin alphabet, they'd write it in IPA. Of course this means different people would write the same word differently, depending on their own personal pronunciation.

A few pages from this newsletter were reprinted in the encyclopedia. The latter has big, glossy high-DPI pages, so they could fit several newsletter pages at reduced size on a page and it was quite readable. I'd learned enough IPA that I could mostly read it -- and it was quite an unusual experience reading this IPA prose, as it felt like I was hearing the person's voice.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-30 18:02 UTC

Sadly (?) at some point the association apparently decided that this wasn't worth the trade-off in terms of people finding it inaccessible to read, and write for, the newsletter. So they switched over to normal orthography.

**Divyanshu Agrawal** · 2020-03-30 18:11 UTC

That's an interesting story! Thanks for sharing.

I was trying to get zulip running directly on macOS without vagrant today. It is possible but the amount of `If MAC_OS` statements it would require along with change in  file paths and a completely new list of dependencies using homebrew would not be worth it.
Posting a document which could be useful if someone attempts this in future which is strictly not recommended from my side. [zulip-mac-direct-setup.pdf](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/ee/du2mG8GRZi_6M--41agLEB49/zulip-mac-direct-setup.pdf)

**Rein Zustand** · 2020-08-03 11:53 UTC

How many `if MAC_OS` statements are there?

**Rein Zustand** · 2020-08-03 12:03 UTC

There is Nix on macOS. If we prepare a nix expression for Zulip dev, we can run on any UNIX system.

**Rein Zustand** · 2020-08-03 12:04 UTC

Some people do actually use Nix instead of Homebrew.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-08-03 15:00 UTC

The major problem is the permission issue in file paths. MacOS is not as forgiving in running executable even under `sudo` compared to linux distros. For example, any folder directly under `/` in not writeable, `usr/bin/` is not allowed to have custom symlinked executables you will have to use `usr/local/bin/`; these two points alone will require our codebase to change massively.

Installing package is not an issue here, homebrew, gem and pip combined can install all the required packages we need.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-03 20:46 UTC

Yeah this is why we haven't supported that in the past... it is a maintenance headache.  The original setup in 2013 did allow it, we just dropped in when zulip was open sourced since it was this terrible set of instructions that took all day.

There can be a lot to learn to get going with LaTeX! I hope you've found some good tools for learning it and working with it.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-27 20:32 UTC

One tool my mathematician friends say is very handy and popular is Overleaf: https://www.overleaf.com/ . Though whether it works well for you may depend on how your Internet connection is doing right now.

A smaller tool that's sometimes very handy (with or without Overleaf) is Detexify: http://detexify.kirelabs.org/classify.html

And then a lower-tech approach for the same job as Detexify is a nice table of symbols :slight_smile: . Here's a [short one](https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/LaTeX:Symbols), which also links to a giant PDF which is good for searching through.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-27 20:38 UTC

The good news is that once you've spent some time learning it, using LaTeX gets a lot faster :chart:. I studied math in college, and we all did our problem sets in LaTeX. Once you know it well, it's faster than writing by hand, if your typing speed is good -- as long as the stuff you're writing doesn't involve diagrams, that is, or super-complicated formulas.

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-03 21:51 UTC

For writing commit messages I don't recommend using either Vim or Emacs, unless you're also using the same editor routinely for lots of other things (or have in the past.)

Both of them are powerful once you've learned lots and lots of corners of how to use them, but are pretty strange and baroque if you haven't spent a lot of time learning all that.

And if the main way you're using them is to write commit messages, it just isn't worth spending that time. (For one thing most commit messages just aren't that complicated, so there's not a lot to be gained from all the fancy things these editors can do.) The most likely outcome is that you won't spend that time -- that even if you plan to, what you'll actually do day by day is spend your time some other way because you correctly perceive it isn't worth it -- and so you'll just keep writing commit messages in a strange and baroque editor.

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-03 21:52 UTC

(I use Emacs, and it's great, but again only if you've spent lots of time over the years to learn it and to customize it.)

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-03 21:54 UTC

The editor I recommend for commit messages, if you don't have another one you like and know well, is Nano: `git config --global core.editor 'nano'`, or `'nano -r68'` to get nice line-wrapping for prose.

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-03 22:43 UTC

@Yash RE ✨ [said](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/65-checkins/topic/RE.20(non.20zulip.20stuff)/near/893984):
> I like vim, it's fun. I'm not confident enough to use it on my IDE via editor bindings. What I'm really hoping to pick up is getting used to stuff like word level and line level actions.

Well, I think you've heard my advice already, then: learning that stuff will take a lot of time, and it won't be worth that time if you're only using it for commit messages. If you find Vim fun, then perhaps what you want to do is to start using it for more things and investing the time to learn it well.

OTOH:

> I feel as though emacs would be faster though, since, well, not an insertion editor.

if you feel you're slow in Vim, that is a good reason to use something else!

My suggestion would be to embrace Nano -- it's a venerable editor that gets right to the point so you can efficiently edit prose. (Its roots are in [an editor for writing email](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pico_(text_editor)), part of an email client which is still a popular choice for people who take email seriously and need to handle a lot of it -- it's the mail client Linus Torvalds uses, and has used for many years.)

You could certainly also use Emacs. In that case I think you'll be happiest in the end if you really spend a lot of time with it. That will only make sense if you use it for more than commit messages.

**Thomas Fini Hansen** · 2020-06-04 06:12 UTC

I think that Greg makes a very good case, but it sounds like Yash would really like to use something else. 

> I feel as though emacs would be faster though, since, well, not an insertion editor.

Emacs is initially easier for most people, whether they come from Notepad, Sublime or a myriad of other editors. Some of it's bindings have even sneaked in elsewhere (ctrl-a/e for beginning/end of line for instance). And commit messages doesn't require much in formatting.

But if that's all you're using it for we have a proverb in danish: shooting sparrows with cannons. If you're not planning on using more Emacs, i would go with Greg and suggest Nano for commit messages. Emacs power shows when you're using it 8 hours a day every day.

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2020-06-04 07:23 UTC

> I'm not confident enough to use it on my IDE via editor bindings.
> What I'm really hoping to pick up is getting used to stuff like word level and line level actions.

Once you get used to stuff like using `ciw` and `ci"` you'll find it hard to use anything other than vim. Vim is strange in the sense that at first it's a bit of a pain to use but then as you learn more and more about what it can do for you and the philosophy behind it (nouns, verbs, and actions), it'll grow on you to the point where you don't really wouldn't  want to work on anything else for any non-trivial work.

A talk that opened me up to what vim is really about is `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wlR5gYd6um0`. It explains how vim is more of an actionable "language" to express the changes you want,

Some other really important features of vim are markers (so that you can easily jump between marks), `e` and `b` (though you can get the same behavior outside of vim with the `ctrl` key), the repeat key,  and tabs and splits.

> I've used vim enough that I hate nano, a little.
  

I can definitely relate.

> learning that stuff will take a lot of time, and it won't be worth that time if you're only using it for commit messages.

I definitely agree with Greg here. Don't learn vim if you want to edit commit messages and stuff.

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2020-06-04 07:25 UTC

Oh, and `zz`/`zt`/`zb` are also really useful.

**Abhigyan Khaund** · 2020-10-03 07:30 UTC

Take care @Trent Lapinski !

**Abhigyan Khaund** · 2020-10-03 07:30 UTC

Your mention of the AQI, really worries me that people in cities like New Delhi (in India) live through AQI of 300+ (sometimes 500+) almost every day for the entire winter months (Oct till Dec/Jan) like its a very normal thing. What deteriorating effect it must be causing!

**Trent Lapinski** · 2020-10-03 22:19 UTC

Thanks. Yeah that’s not good that so many people breathe this kind of air quality regularly. 

Ours is due to acute smoke exposure vs. pollution. So it’s not necessarily smoke inhalation in some of these cities but rather a combination of factors.

They’re both unhealthy of course, but smoke inhalation is acute in its health effects. What’s in the smoke / bad air and it’s relative toxicity is a factor. 

Overall though the health effects of breathing high AQI air are well documented as having negative impacts on brain function, mental acuity, immune function, etc.

**Greg Price** · 2020-10-05 19:40 UTC

A few years ago I was in Delhi in November -- just for a couple of days en route to elsewhere in India -- and the AQI was I think 500+. It was really bad -- we could feel the smoke in our noses and mouths, and everything looked hazy even a few tens of meters away. Anything a kilometer away was invisible in the haze.

I believe most of that was smoke from people burning the stubble left on fields after harvest. So the makeup of it may be not very different from what we've had with the wildfires here.

**Greg Price** · 2020-10-05 19:46 UTC

I'm sure it does have significant health effects for many people in places like Delhi. I saw an estimate from public-health researchers here that the wildfire smoke this season will have caused a few thousand more people in California to die that wouldn't have otherwise. And for most people in California (for people in the most densely populated areas) it never got quite as bad as I experienced in Delhi, and it was bad for a much shorter period. So it probably causes many more deaths there each year.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-05 23:18 UTC

Yeah, air pollution is well understood to be a significant factor in variation of life expectancy between different places.

Hi, for the last few days, I've been working on optimizing Zulip on Chrome mobile browser (right now, Zulip is almost unusable on Chrome mobile). After a few days of research, it turned out that Chrome is creating multiple composite layers when Zulip is being run on mobile which is causing layer invalidation and long "update layer tree" operations every time we scroll. I'll post more details with reference articles when I open a PR for this.

I am currently working on fixing this which will hopefully make scrolling smooth on Chrome mobile. After that, I'll get back to the end-to-end encryption project.

**Cyphase** · 2020-06-08 01:14 UTC

Hello #**checkins**!

A brief intro since this is my first checkin. I've been active here on CZO since late-April 2019 when I set up a self-hosted Zulip server for a community center I'm involved with, though I'd been aware of Zulip long before that. Up until last week I'd participated here and a bit on GitHub, including opening some issues. But [now](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/8-commits/topic/zulip.20.2F.20master/near/892152) I've [finally](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/8-commits/topic/zulip.20.2F.20master/near/892334) [contributed](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/8-commits/topic/zulip.20.2F.20master/near/892483) [some code](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/8-commits/topic/zulip.20.2F.20master/near/898237)! :confetti: 

* #15161 fixed a stale sentence in the team page.
* #15169 and #15170 were documentation fixes.
* #15249 fixed a few UI issues in the edit history modal, along with doing some refactoring and cleanup. I guess @Tim Abbott [really liked](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/14-GSoC/topic/writing.20good.20commits/near/898239) the commit messages; I appreciate that!

I've been taking my time so far, taking tangents when they present themselves and getting a better feel for the codebase, style conventions, etc. While I already knew that Zulip had great code, documentation, and developer tooling, I've gained a new appreciation for it! :octopus:

Next up, after I fix some documentation issues I noticed while working on #15249, is more edit history work. The edit history code doesn't know anything about stream edits – although the message edit code does save the previous stream in the edit history entry at edit-time – so I plan to add that support, which will mean my first backend changes; I also have some UI/UX ideas to consider; and I want to see if, where, and when adding frontend edit history tests might be appropriate, as there currently aren't any.

I'm looking forward to more Zulip development in the future!

P.S. After having had 4k+ unreads [ten days ago](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/9-issues/topic/webapp.20lag/near/889813), I'm down to 1246 total unreads as I post this. Getting closer!

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-24 14:17 UTC

For #15542 do we want to distinguish `mobile-mode` from `thin-mode`?  I think `mobile-mode` is probably the right decision here, but I think there are situations where "thin mode" is really a better way to describe it, since the setting isn't particularly driven by being on a mobile device, and it could just be that you have a narrow browser window.  I don't have a strong opinion here--I think there's an argument that if this setting applies to mobile mode in 95% of the cases, that's just a better way to express it.  Thoughts?

**Thomas Fini Hansen** · 2020-06-24 14:56 UTC

> I think mobile-mode is probably the right decision here, but I think there are situations where "thin mode" is really a better way to describe it, since the setting isn't particularly driven by being on a mobile device, and it could just be that you have a narrow browser window.

This article makes the same point: https://mattanddesign.com/dont-design-for-mobile/ and I dig it... Having buttons blow up just because you resized the window down is a bit of an annyance, but it means you'll have to account for more combinations.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-24 15:01 UTC

Perhaps `thin-viewport` would be a better name here?  (Thanks for the link, @Thomas Fini Hansen)

The double dashes are [custom CSS properties](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Using_CSS_custom_properties), these are directly supported by browsers (which is useful since you see them when inspecting with the developer tools).

## ETA on 4.0?

*2020-12-16 to 2021-01-26 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/65-checkins/topic/ETA.20on.204.2E0.3F/with/1082153)*

**Matt Hall** · 2020-12-16 23:32 UTC

Hello, just wondering when 4.0 is expected to be released and if there is anything on the server side I should prepare for the upgrade. Thanks!

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-12-16 23:48 UTC

@Matt Hall we don't have a date set, but in any case there isn't anything special you'll need to do for that upgrade.  You can always run master if you want features not yet in 4.0 -- we work hard to keep it stable (because that's what we run in Zulip Cloud, among other reasons).

**mouk** · 2021-01-26 19:57 UTC

An update here would be nice :-)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-01-26 20:05 UTC

We haven’t planned the timing for the 4.0 release yet, but we encourage you to [upgrade from Git](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/production/upgrade-or-modify.html#upgrading-from-a-git-repository) if you’re interested in the new features there. (You cannot downgrade from Git to a previous release, but you will be able to upgrade from Git to the next release when it’s available.)

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-12-19 12:26 UTC

A couple months ago, I had moved away from Windows 10 on my laptop and installed Ubuntu 20.04 LTS (without dual-boot). I was using WSL2 earlier on Windows. When it came to installing the development environment on Linux, the Vagrant installation method Just Worked :smile:.

I hadn't expected to being able to get into my earlier edit-debug cycle so quickly! I still need to set the bash and git aliases though.

I do feel a noticeable increase in performance -- I can now easily run the development server + Firefox + VS Code along with a couple other unrelated apps (Music Player, etc) without any noticeable stutter. As a Windows user, I sometimes had to go as far as closing down VS Code before starting the development server; things were just so sluggish.

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2023-06-13 04:31 UTC

Hi all! I had planned a vacation from 2nd June to 18th June in the Himalayas. The first week went well and I enjoyed every bit of it. 
Unfortunately, due to changing climate around me because of travel, I fell ill after the first week (around 10th June) with a throat infection and subsequently fever.
I had to cancel the second part of part of the vacation, which was supposed to be my first ever Himalayan trek (something to do only when one is totally fit), so I was very much disappointed :(
I'm back home right now, and recovering.

I've been raised up and lived in the hot/humid climate of the [Mumbai Metropolitan region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai_Metropolitan_Region) for almost all my life, so I'm used to neither the cold/dry climate in the Himalayas, nor the hot/dry climate near [Delhi NCR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Capital_Region_(India)), which is on-the-way. So I guess me falling sick was something I should have expected. Anyways, I'll try to take more precautions next time, and am looking for more generic ways to increase my immunity.

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-01 21:16 UTC

The side effects certainly vary from person to person, but there's a general trend that older people have weaker side effects than younger people. This is explained as being related to people's immune systems getting weaker as they age -- the common side effects are caused by the immune response.

For example here's a description of side effects seen in a study of the Pfizer vaccine:
https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/covid-19/info-by-product/pfizer/reactogenicity.html
42% of people 18-55 years old who got the vaccine reported a headache,
vs 25% of people >55 years old.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-07 17:05 UTC

I think the right way to think about GitHub stars is that they are basically the sum of a thing that's useful to measure (people who like an open source project and want to follow it) and a measure of the total "press" traffic a project's GitHub homepage, which is basically irrelevant in that a repository that's effectively an interesting blog post has similar relevance for attracting stars as a project that tons of people work on and use (in part because those two types of things are equally likely to get "press" from Hacker News / Reddit / etc.).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-07 17:08 UTC

So if you see a project that only has 30 stars, you can be pretty sure that it's not important/popular, but inference in the other direction doesn't work.

**Alya Abbott** · 2021-04-19 22:22 UTC

Checking in after 3 weeks at Zulip! It's a length of time that somehow feels really short and like it's been forever at the same time.

1. It's been great to spend time with folks going through the high-priority mobile backlog. It's definitely educational for me -- e.g., I hadn't previously thought much about just how difficult it is to create a seamless-feeling experience when the device may or may not have an internet connection at any given time.

2. I'm starting to reach out to a few customers... It's really nice to talk to people who are doing things that just wouldn't be possible if Zulip didn't exist. For example, I talked to a math professor who decided to open up his graduate-level class to anyone around the world, and has been able to use Zulip to effectively manage the discussion and questions even though his students are scattered across all continents other than Antarctica. It's also been interesting to go though the list of organizations that are signing up for Zulip and get a feel for the really wide variety of groups that are finding and trying out Zulip.

3. I'm excited about the current state of our customer support (kudos to @Mateusz Mandera !), and I think with @Aman Agrawal (amanagr)  and me helping out, we should be able to be responsive and avoid dropping threads when @Tim Abbott gets too busy with other priorities. :)

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-06-22 20:36 UTC

Seems like about time for another checkin :)

I've been focused on performance for the past week and a bit. I've found a few exciting avenues of performance improvement:

* I investigated the webview loading time, and shaved ~58ms off on average (#M4804)
* But I want to do a lot more than that, so I've started investigating keeping a webview loaded all the time, so we can take the ~250ms webview load time to 0ms. I've made some promising progress on that (#M4808, #**mobile-team>#M4808 — hot webviews**)
* Doing all that gave me a pretty good understanding of where the bottlenecks are in the webview code, which should let us further improve load times: #M4806
* I also figured out how to improve our React Native list performance, which should make scrolling through the home screen and various other lists nicer. Check out [these](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/243-mobile-team/topic/getItemLayout/near/1212638) before and after videos for the sort of improvement this is :) I have a prototype PR (#M4809) to do this for a different list, but it's waiting on a native module that I need to write (#**mobile-team>text height**), which is in turn waiting on the MacBook I ordered arriving.
* #M4821 is a small change, but it should make the "N unread messages" bar significantly more responsive, which I'm excited about.
* I also opened #M4813 to add a tiny animation to the "scroll to bottom" button. I'm hoping to add more animations to our app in general, to help make it feel a bit nicer to use.

I also made a couple small tactical fixes to help with P1 bugs:

* #M4817 to help with a bug causing the app to crash when users try to open a notification, which mostly affected self-hosted users.
* #M4807 to show muted messages in the "mentions" narrow

**Palash Raghuwanshi** · 2021-12-08 13:54 UTC

Today I learned how to get all the variables passed to a hbs template.
1. git grep <insert-name-of-the-template>, go to the js template that uses that template.
2. Look at the imports of that js file, a function would have been imported from our template in question.
3. Find where that function has been used, you'll see variables passed to it, just use the `console.log(variable)` to see them.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-15 00:47 UTC

(replying to shlok (madrix01))
> setting up my new Emacs work environment(any tips?)

My best Emacs tip isn't in the environment setup, exactly, but in how you use it:

When you press a keychord like C-x or M-x, don't do it with one hand. Do it with two: the X with your left hand, and the Ctrl or Alt/Option/Meta with your right hand.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-15 00:49 UTC

For me, switching to that approach made things a lot easier on my wrists. The X is so close to the Ctrl and Alt keys (on a typical QWERTY keyboard, at least) that hitting C-x or M-x with just the left hand involves cramping the fingers together in a way that, at least for my hands, wasn't good for the wrist.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-15 00:51 UTC

As a bonus, I think sequences like C-x C-s are actually faster for me this way, because hitting X with the index finger followed by S with the middle finger is an extremely natural and quick sequence.

That's a great one! I definitely remind myself of this whenever I feel like it took me a really long time to do something because I'm new to it. (Unless it's Git, in which case I just get grumpy instead. :stuck_out_tongue_wink: )

Even if lots of other people could have done it faster, it can still be a great investment for you to spend the time to figure it out. That's true even if you take a narrow "how can I best help Zulip?" perspective, which means you definitely shouldn't feel about about taking the time to work through something if it helps you learn skills/knowledge that will help you down the line.

**Alya Abbott** · 2021-12-23 04:47 UTC

I haven't been using this technique at Zulip, but in my previous job, it really helped me to put pretty much everything I was doing on a todo list, and check it off when it was done. This included things that might seem small, like "read doc X" or "give feedback on proposal Y" or "schedule a meeting to discuss Z".

The two main benefits were that it mean that I rarely dropped the ball on some follow-up I needed to do, but also that it made it much more tangible that I was getting things done. Tasks like the ones above might not feel like accomplishments, but they still take time and represent progress.

The spreadsheet I used also had a "category" column for the type of task it is (e.g. reading, reviews, logistics, etc.), which was mildly useful for skimming for the type of task I was in the mood for, and was also somehow helpful for not feeling silly about writing down things that might seem small or don't produce a tangible output.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-23 11:53 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell (showell))
> One piece of advice that I sometimes give folks is to occasionally allow yourself an hour (set the timer on your phone if it helps) to just focus on reading code and exploring.
 
I should probably clarify that the "one hour" aspect of this suggestion is fairly arbitrary.  You could allocate an entire day every N days to just reading and exploring, especially if you're the kind of person who can stay in the zone for a long time.  The reason I suggest an hour, and using the timer, is that you'll often be surprised in either direction when the hour ends up, and it can be a positive surprise in either direction.  If the time flies by faster than you think, then it might help you appreciate just how much time is spent during other periods of non-measured/non-focused time to reading, searching, and exploring, and that can help you feel less rushed and make better time estimates.  And then occasionally it's the opposite--the hour seems like forever, and you have covered a ton of ground, and you realize how much you can learn when you're not distracted by the pressure of executing some immediate task.

Obviously, a lot depends on your personality type and your natural rhythms.  For example, I am a morning person, so I try to do execution-oriented things in the morning, and then I do more outside-the-box kind of things in the afternoon.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-30 18:30 UTC

The two features I very frequently use other than those in the post are:
* Showing a bit of context around each match: `-C`, e.g. `git grep -C2 mandatory_topics -- zerver/`. You can also get different numbers of lines after and before the match: `-A4 -B2` gives 4 lines after and 2 lines before.
* Matching only when the pattern is the whole word: `-w`, e.g. `git grep -w mandatory_topics -- zerver/` which no longer matches occurrences of "realm_mandatory_topics". Often very handy when the thing you're looking for is an identifier.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-30 18:36 UTC

If you wanted to cut something, probably `-c` (counts) is the most dispensable. In the post's own example, `-l` (list of files) is more direct for doing what you actually needed. I use `-l` reasonably often, but rarely find a use for `-c`.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-30 18:39 UTC

(replying to Yash RE)
> You could consider mentioning `git log --grep` as in `git log --oneline --grep="emoji"`, I'm not certain that you'd want to, but it's definitely something that IDE search can't do.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-30 18:53 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> Neat! I hadn't known about `--break` and `--heading`. In my own usage, I've mostly switched to using `rg` instead of `git grep`. I do that even though the actual search behavior of `rg` is slightly less helpful than that of `git grep`

OK, and in case anyone else finds it helpful: here's the block I've just added to my `~/.gitconfig`!
```ini
# `git grep` configuration.
[alias]
        # Alias to get `rg`-style nice output with `git grep` precision.
        g = grep --break --heading --line-number
[grep]
        # "Basic" regexps are a relic.  Extended would be fine; Perl is better.
        patternType = perl
[color "grep"]
        # Get some colors on those headings and line numbers, to help
        # set them apart from the text.
        filename = magenta
        lineNumber = green
```

Now `git g` gives me the same nice format of output as `rg`. :smiley:

Hey everyone, It's been a very long (understatement) since my last check-in. So here are my recent updates (~ 1 month),

- ** #28799 hotkey: Add `Shift` + `V` keyboard shortcut for the read receipts menu. **

- ** #29061 message_list_tooltips: Add "View bot card" tooltips for bots. **
- ** #28523 compose_tooltips: Improve tooltips logic for compose-closed UI. **
- ** #29194 compose: Fix topics required banner closing on enter to send. **
- ** #29213 navbar: Add navigate to home view tooltip to the organization logo. **

### :git-pull-request-open:  Open PRs
- ** #29107 redesign: Message actions menu **
  This PR will server as the base for all other popover redesigns. The PR commits to convert the currently used navbar styling into a general popover menu styling, accounting for any additional design changes we want to append on top. I'm currently waiting for some clarification in #**design>UI redesign: message actions menu popover #29107**  and for the message source icon over at #**design>view message source icon**.
- ** #29249 personal_menu: Add theme switcher to personal menu popover. **
  This PR is ready for a design discussion on whether we want a sliding animation on the theme switcher, before it's ready for a review. If you have some opinion/concern regarding the same, please feel free to join the discussion at #**design>UI redesign: theme switcher #22803**.

### :zulip_dev: Work in-progress
- Haven't planned on the next steps at the moment. My initial inclination is towards working on the other popover redesigns tasks over at #28699, by rebasing off of the prep commits in #29107. This would allow for successive quick PRs once #29107 gets merged.

### :shrug: Others
(mostly regarding the [Zulip 9.0 priorities board](https://github.com/orgs/zulip/projects/9/views/1))

So should I prioritize to get this done earlier? FYI @Tim Abbott.

Since this helper will enable checking the highlighted selection / cursor position as well, the tests have become a lot more thorough, and I've already found and fixed a couple bugs thanks to the new tests! I hope to be ready with a review ready iteration of this project by tomorrow :fingers_crossed: Till then here's a peak at the new tests:
```javascript
// Link selected text
init_textarea_state("before <abc> after");
compose_ui.format_text($textarea, "link");
assert.equal(get_textarea_state(), "before [abc](<url>) after");
```

This week I worked on Panel-follows-Narrow, a zulip-terminal ux design principle that we're trying to enforce wherein the side panel, which contains all of the navigation tools for the streams and topics, will change to follow what has been narrowed to. 

The first step of this was highlighting the current stream, which I did, and then I adapted one of. my previous WIP PRs to open a list of topics below the selected stream with top N (currently 3) topics. I'm working on adapting the highlighting to topics, and to change the panel from streams to topics and back whenever the user narrows from one to the other.

## organizing checkins

*2023-04-13 to 2023-04-13 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/65-checkins/topic/organizing.20checkins/with/1547327)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-13 20:26 UTC

For folks who have a bunch of in-progress work and thus have long checkins that mention a half-dozen issues/PRs, I think it'd be really helpful for folks to use a format with a few sections, rather than having everything jumbled together. I'm currently thinking 3 sections would be helpful:
* Merged work: Items that are merged. These are great to include so folks can celebrate the progress.
* Work awaiting review: These are items where you've resolved all feedback yourself, and I or @Alya Abbott when reading the checkin might use it as a reminder of something that's close to completion and where a review might let us close it out. It's probably best to sort these by who you expect the next reviewer to be if there's more than a couple in this category.
* What you're working on: These are great for sharing with the community your plans (and whether you're looking for more projects!), and often can be opportunities for someone to do an early review or provide some feedback that they think of when seeing you're working on it, but aren't ready for a main review.

Thoughts? I think even just organizing the part of checkins that contain lists of issues into 3 bulleted lists with those headings (if all of those categories exist) would really help me. If folks like the idea, we can potentially make a copyable template or otherwise document it further.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2023-04-13 22:55 UTC

This sounds useful, and should be fairly simple to follow once we get started :+1:

It may not be warranted for this alone, but a more general feature to provide a template to fill in - like a PR or issue template - could be useful for this at some point? I had a quick look, but didn't see an issue for that, though I vaguely recall feedback along these lines too.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-13 23:31 UTC

There's a "saved replies" concept we've thought about in the past, but nothing that would be a template. We could pretty easily have something to copy linked to from the stream description, though.

#24338: popovers: Fix hide all popovers when clicked on search or settings. Though, it was awaiting review for a long time, I updated it recently to fix the errors that occurred after rebase.
#24367: css: Fix dropdown text alignment centered. A recent discussion on this kind of finalized what we want to do and, updated it in the PR.
#24612: popovers: Fix hide popovers during scroll in recent conversations. This one is I think, ready to be merged. Plus, it got only one line change so will be quick to review.
#24684: search: Add filter section for direct messages. `Tim Abbott` left some comments on this one. I think I've addressed them and now the PR is ready to be merged.

**Pending Review**
#24832: docs: Advertise using git grep to find things. I added docs for `git grep` in this one. First time adding docs for Zulip.
#24934: notifications: Fix blank notification sent when no text specified. When we send a message (in dms) with link to an image but not label, it triggered an empty notification. Added `Sent this file.` as text if there is none.
 #25059: search: Add appropriate error for misused search operators. Recently worked on this one to show appropriate messages when we search with an invalid `operator: operand` combination.
#25135: search: Fix display of suggestion box when search bar empty.  Recently reported and worked on this one. Solved this by modifying `typeahead.js` according to our needs.

**In Progress**
#25014: Working on a jump-to-date feature where we can select on the message which date we'd like to jump. Also, there will be a scroll to the top button. I am trying to figure out some errors that arise when we try to interact with the `fratpickr` with keyboard`. Like, using arrow keys to select a date and hitting enter. Also, trying to figure out how to update `tippy` since the text of tippy is added by `timerender.js` and not `tippy.js`.

After I am done with the current one in progress, I am planning to take on the issue around the addition of notifications for alert words which is also a part of my proposal. `Prakhar Pratyush` also has this as part of their proposal. I think we might want to collaborate on this one if required.

Ok, even only writing this is giving clarity to me on where I'm at. I didn't realize this before.

Thanks for sparing some time to give it a read :heart:

## :magnifying_glass: Investigated Issue
Hi @Tim Abbott , I noticed you mentioned the idea of pre-populating incoming webhook bots with their **bot avatars** in [ISSUE#692](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/692), [PR#12474](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/12474). From what I can infer, it seems like it's a big UI improvement we've wanted for a long time but some prerequisites were pending back then. I'm curious if this feature is actionable now. I couldn't find a recent CZO discussion  nor GitHub issue addressing this feature specifically. 

I'm interested in this specific issue because by the byproduct of solving this issue is maybe a proper way of interacting with `BotConfigData` and thus extended capabilities of configuring incoming webhook bots in general. It could pave way for other integration related features I've been following so far, such as the continuation of [PR#12109](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/12109) to implement **`http_api_callback()`** and after that, **refactoring of external integration helper scripts** into the main code base is also a possible improvement. Which would ultimately benefit integrations such as: ClickUp, Trello, BitBucket, Stripe, Phabircator(?), Twitter(?) 

I wonder about the relevancy of these issues. If you think any of them is worth investigating further, I'm interested in converting them into a proper set of PR and issue. Or, if there are any higher priority or relevant issue for me to work on, please do let me know!

**Aman (whilstsomebody)** · 2025-04-13 18:04 UTC

Hello folks!
This Saturday was very exciting and busy for me. Our college hosted a grand meet by the [FOSS United Foundation](https://fossunited.org/) which lasted for about 8 hours. This was organized for the first time in our college, and both I and @Maneesh Shukla attended it. In fact, @Maneesh Shukla was part of the organizing team responsible for the smooth conduction of the event.

The event featured many experienced and well-known personalities who have achieved benchmarks in FOSS.
The event consisted of several talks, with some major ones being:

* Speaker session on [IntentJs - A new Node.js framework](https://github.com/intentjs)
* Practical Guide on Monitoring Microservices with [Grafana](https://grafana.com/)
* Workshops on Functional Programming with the Elixir Language
* Coordinating a Windows 10 to Linux upcycling by [Joseph P. De Veaugh-Geiss - Manager at KDE eco](https://www.sfscon.it/speakers/joseph-p-de-veaugh-geiss/)
* Introduction to [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/) by Contrapunctus

At the end, we had a Fireside chat with [Kailash Nadh](https://in.linkedin.com/in/kailashnadh) - CTO at [Zerodha](https://zerodha.com/).

Overall, it was a great experience full of knowledgeable talks and knowledgeable people. I hope I can attend more sessions like this in the future.

**Maneesh Shukla** · 2025-04-14 14:31 UTC

Absolutely! It was truly a great experience hearing such people.
One of the most motivating moment of the day was during a casual conversation with Zerodha's CTO, Kailash Nadh, while he was having tea with us. He mentioned that he had worked for 25 hours last weekend (Saturday & Sunday).

As a college student, it sometimes feels disheartening to spend weekends working while others are out enjoying. But hearing that from someone at this level made me feel energized and motivated to work even harder over the weekends.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-04-16 00:17 UTC

Working 25 hours over a weekend is a lifestyle choice -- I've had times in my life when I did that and had a lot of fun working long hours -- though I don't think it was ever that long -- the original Ksplice work hours were 10 hrs/day, 6 days/week. But I think it's only a reasonable thing to do if you're enjoying the time -- E.g., when I did work on the weekend, I'd usually pick things to work on that would be emotionally satisfying, rather than what's the highest priority.

These days, with young kids, that's neither feasible nor is what I'm excited to do with my weekends.

- docs: Update `sending-messages.md` and `markdown.md` for variable/function updates - [#32799](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/32799).

- settings UI: Improve UI for email changes - [#32260](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/32260).
- settings: Use text cursor for "Name" and "Email" field labels (if changes are disabled) - [#32622](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/32622).

---

:git-pull-request-open: **Open PRs:**
- popovers: Fix layout bugs in the help modal - [#31466](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/31466) (awaiting review from @Karl Stolley - my first PR :smile:).

- bots: Add a setting to customize the Welcome Bot message - [#32862](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/32862).

--- 

I would like to mention some things that I like most about Zulip:
- The codebase has taught me a lot about how to write good quality code, specifically, the well-structured and modularized format, following code reusability, code extensibility, and abstraction. 
- The tooltips and the pill format used like user pills, and channel pills are my favorite.
- The keyboard shortcuts and documentation are really helpful.
- The discussions in different channels provide a vast amount of info on the evolving application and codebase.
- And yes, the people here are great.

---

Well, I would like to thank Zulip and the people here for this.

Hello everyone, I hope you are doing great.
---

Lately, I have had something in mind, and I would really like to share it with this community, which has given me so much that I can't even express my gratitude in words. This post might be a bit long, so you are welcome to skip this.
---

So, I started looking into GSoC around July-August 2024, and at that time, I was very new to open source. One of my hostel friends, @Kunal Sharma, had already contributed to Zulip under GSoC in 2024. So, I decided, let's give it a shot. When coming back to the hostel, after my holidays, I discussed this with @Kumar Aniket, he was on the same track. So, I remember, I joined Zulip on 7 August 2024. I would browse through the messages, look at how people talked, how they asked for help, what mistakes I should not make, and so on. I opened my first PR: *popovers: Fix alignment of Time example output in Message formatting pane - #31466*, on 28 August 2024. My first PR, which was merged, was: popovers: *Refactor resend and revoke invitation confirmation modals - #31896*, I remember I was beyond happy and just ran straight away into @Kunal Sharma 's room, told him about it, yes, it was really great.
---

After that, it was sort of a roller coaster ride. Sometimes, it was late nights, just looking at my screen and comprehending, okay, what is going on, since it was my first time working on this big project. Sometimes, I was just like damn, I solved the bug, finally. We 3 (Aniket, Kunal, and I) were always discussing what reviews we received, how we addressed them, and helping each other out. To be honest, that time was the most beautiful time of my GSoC journey. I mean, yes, the result day was, to be honest, very suspenseful, since we 3 had all applied; if anyone wasn't selected for GSoC, it would be very sad for all of us. We used to discuss what we would do if any of us didn't get selected, or, best case, all 3 of us did, and luckily, we all were selected.
---

After GSoC started, I was very motivated at the start. I was like, okay, let's wrap up all my work as quickly as possible, and then I would have free time during my college placements. But, to be honest, due to procrastination, I believe I didn't give 100% to it. Did I give my 100% before GSoC? Yes, I did. Did I do it after GSoC? No, and honestly, I sometimes feel kind of like letting people down for that. When my college started after the vacations, in July, the placement season started. So, I became very busy with it. In the following time, I had to extend my GSoC project, since I wasn't able to commit the work hours, which I should have been committing to the project. It felt quite bad, since, before GSoC, I was willing to go above and beyond, but post-GSoC, things became quite different.
---

I wrapped up my GSoC on October 27. Did I wrap it up successfully? Yes. Am I satisfied with my work, umm, no. Should I have put more effort? Yes, again yes.
I don't know if I have enough credibility to say this for future contributors to any outreach programs like GSoC. But I would like to share something.
---

While I was quite stressed about my placements and all, I decided to take a diversion for a while. I tried to look for other organizations in GSoC. I couldn't find any organization as welcoming as Zulip. I am not saying that there is no other organization like Zulip, since I only browsed the GSoC organizations having a tech stack similar to mine.
I don't know if I am able to express myself or not, but the little things that everyone cares about here are very big.
Take, for example, the documentation, I mean, it is like a goldmine for us devs.
Take, for example, the channel where you are posting your message.
Take, for example, how you start a thread in #**api design**.
Take, for example, the commit discipline. I remember violating it in my first PR at that time. I was like, it's just a commit, why need to bother so much about it?
But the thing is, when people care about these little things, it helps build something like Zulip. I spent around 3-4 days looking for organizations, going to their codebases, mailing lists, discussions, etc., but couldn't find a welcoming community like Zulip. So, for any future contributors out there, please make the most out of your program.

See, I do understand, for other organizations; it is their way of working things out, and I have no right to comment on it. The thing I want to say is I am very grateful to Zulip for this journey, and I should have contributed more. I have tons of stories to tell people. I tell it to my family, my cousins, my school friends, and my interviewers also :).
---

What I wanted to share is that, although it was an amazing experience contributing to Zulip before GSoC. After GSoC, it didn't go as well as it should have. And honestly, I apologise for that, since I let people down.

I would love to be a part of Zulip, even in the coming days, contributing to it when I get time, in any way, may it is resolving some minor issues or helping fellow devs.
I just want to express my gratitude to Zulip for this great chapter of my life.
Thanks again, people @ Zulip.

**Greg Price** · 2025-03-19 23:15 UTC

Our [list of GSoC project ideas](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/outreach/gsoc.html) has a description of the specific kinds of subprojects to try in the REST API docs:
> Zulip’s [**REST API documentation**](https://zulip.com/api/), which is an important resource for any organization integrating with Zulip, as well as the developers of our API clients. Zulip has a [nice framework](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/documentation/api.html) for writing API documentation built by past GSoC students based on the OpenAPI standard with built-in automated tests of the data both the Python and curl examples. However, the documentation isn’t yet what we’re hoping for: there are a few dozen endpoints that are missing, several of which are quite important, the visual design isn’t perfect (especially for, e.g., `GET /events`), many templates could be deleted with a bit of framework effort, etc. See the [API docs area label](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3A%22area%3A+documentation+%28api+and+integrations%29%22) for some specific projects in the area; and `git grep pending_endpoints` to find the list of endpoints that need documentation and their priorities. Our goal for the summer is for 1-2 students to resolve all open issues related to the REST API documentation. 175 or 350 hours; difficulty easy or medium. **Skills required**: Python programming. Expertise with reading documentation and English writing are valuable, and product thinking about the experience of using third-party APIs is very helpful.

**Greg Price** · 2025-03-19 23:17 UTC

Documenting specific endpoints generally requires a lot less background expertise than writing from scratch an article like the one called for in #10415.

Instead you'd pick an endpoint and study in detail how it works so as to become an expert on that very specific question: what's the interface of this endpoint. Then you can write its documentation.

**Greg Price** · 2025-03-19 23:19 UTC

And the other general theme of that project idea is about work on the docs framework, rather than writing docs.

**Niloth** · 2025-03-22 16:59 UTC

All of those answers are available in the first page of the Contributing Guide. There are 6 mentions of the "help wanted" label in that page.

Where to look for an issue
> You can look through issues tagged with the “help wanted” label, which is used to indicate the issues that are open for contributions.

Picking an issue to work on
> Find an issue tagged with the “help wanted” label that is either unassigned, or looks to be abandoned.

Claiming an issue
> If the issue is tagged with a help wanted label and is not assigned to someone else, Zulipbot will immediately assign the issue to you.

Other mentions
> find an issue labeled “help wanted”, and only pick up one issue at a time to start with.

> you can also find another “help wanted” issue in the same area to work on.

The "help wanted" labels in zulip/zulip and python-zulip-api do not have an attached description.

**Greg Price** · 2025-03-22 21:16 UTC

Apart from the question of whether an issue has the "help wanted" label or not, I think the key point in the contributing guide (included in what @Alya Abbott quoted above) is:
> If picking up a bug, start by checking if you can replicate it. If it no longer replicates, post a comment on the issue explaining how you tested the behavior, and what you saw, with screenshots as appropriate. And if you *can* replicate it, fixing it is great!

So for example if you're looking at #22937, which begins:
> When I try to generate a client using the official openapi yaml file in zerver/openapi/zulip.yaml, I get the following error:
> […]
> The same error appears in https://editor.swagger.io.

and want to find out if it's still relevant, the way to do that is to try to generate a client using that OpenAPI YAML file, and see if that still produces a similar error today.

If it does, then clearly the issue still applies. If it doesn't, then maybe it doesn't; and posting your findings in detail can help toward deciding if that's the case.

**Greg Price** · 2025-03-22 21:18 UTC

Similarly, for an issue like #10415 or #32103 or #25443 which is asking for some docs to be written, the way to confirm whether it's still relevant is to look for existing docs that cover the area.

**What I worked on:**
I implemented the ability for admins and bot owners to change a bot's `short_name` (the first part of the bot's email, e.g., `cookie` in `cookie-bot@zulipdev.com`). This feature enables reusing deactivated bots that may be taking up desired names.

**Fixes:** https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/34604

**Adarsh Pandey** · 2026-02-16 18:18 UTC

**Why I chose Zulip**
**Zulip stood out to me**: My entry into Zulip started from curiosity about how large, real-world systems are built and maintained in open-source. What stood out to me quickly about Zulip was how intuitive and easy communication on Zulip was, where everything was segregated first into channels and then into topics, allowing for manageable productive conversations.

**Helpful docs and community**: Despite the size of the project, the detailed and structured documentation, patient and constructive community, educational reviews and insightful discussions, make it a highly positive experience contributing to Zulip.

**My experience**: This was also my first time contributing this actively to open source, so there was some initial hesitation - figuring out issue selection, contribution norms, and communication patterns. That uncertainty faded quickly thanks to how thoughtful the community is. Reviews here don’t just correct code - they teach systems thinking.

**My Contributions**
 :git-merge: **Merged:**
- **inbox_ui**: Update empty state text for "followed topics" filter [#37191](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37191)

:smiley_cat: **In Progress:**

- **emails**: Improve header bars colors and borders in digest emails. [#37289](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37289). Under review by @Prakhar Pratyush.
- **settings**: Add padding for non-square emojis. [#37571](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37571). Addressed latest feedback. Ready for review by @Alya Abbott.
- **read-receipt**: Convert read-receipt modal to popover. [#37683](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37683). Ready for review by @Alya Abbott.
- **submessages**: Add timestamp field to persist event times. [#37839](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37839). Addressed latest feedback. Ready for review by @Greg Price.
- **portico**: Fix case studies menu overflow on low-height screens. [#37880](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37880). Working on the latest feedback by @Aman (amanagr).

[#37231](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37231) - closed in favor of [#37571](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37571) after discussion on the [CZO](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/allow.20cropping.20when.20uploading.20custom.20emojis.20.2337231/with/2349329) over the root cause of this issue.


**Beyond code**
Alongside PR work, I’ve helped other folks in the community by linking active PRs to issues when they weren’t visible in GitHub due to description formatting, flagging unresolved conflicts that block reviews, and helping newer contributors navigate workflows or conventions when I could.

**Gratitude**
I sincerely appreciate the maintainers for the depth and clarity of reviews, especially in cases where my first approach missed the mark. Those discussions ended up being some of the most educational moments.

Also enjoy reading everyone else’s check-ins here, seeing parallel progress across different parts of the codebase is genuinely motivating.

**Current focus**
Lately I’ve been spending more time around the messaging feed and rendering surfaces, understanding how message models, events, and UI layers interact, and how changes propagate through that pipeline.

Plan is to keep going deeper in this area, picking up issues that touch message lifecycle, event visibility, and rendering behavior, while continuing to build a stronger mental model of how these systems fit together internally.
